THE COMPLETE STUDY OF 72 MELAKARTA RĀGAS AND 22 ŚRUTIS

Cross-Referenced with Dīkṣitar's & Śyāma Śāstri's Kṛtis and Śaṅkarācārya's Metaphorical Literature: Sanskrit as the Healing Language of Body, Mind, and Soul

284
PREFACE

PREFACE

Pages i–xx

I. Genesis of This Work

This work was born from a singular conviction — a conviction shared by the ancient ṛṣis who first heard the Veda, by the grammarians who first mapped the architecture of Sanskrit, by the musicians who first organized the ocean of sound into the rivers of rāga, and by the philosophers who first recognized that the ultimate reality is not silence but a vibration so profound that it contains all silence within itself. That conviction is this: Sound heals.

Not metaphorically. Not poetically. Not as a pleasant adjunct to "real" medicine. Sound heals — directly, materially, comprehensively — at every level of the human being: the physical body with its organs and tissues, the subtle body with its emotions and thoughts, and the causal body with its karmic impressions and existential ignorance.

This conviction is not mine alone. It belongs to a tradition that stretches back at least five thousand years — from the Ṛg Vedic hymns to Vāc (Speech), through Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and its systematic exposition of the 22 Śrutis, through Veṅkaṭamakhi's mathematical derivation of the 72 Melakarta system, through the luminous compositions of Muttuswāmi Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri, and through the philosophical literature of Ādi Śaṅkarācārya that provides the ultimate context for understanding why sound heals and what healing truly means.

What is new in this work is not the conviction itself but the synthesis — the attempt to bring together, within a single comprehensive framework, three domains that are usually studied separately:

  1. The 22 Śrutis — the microtonal intervals that constitute the atomic structure of Indian music

  2. The 72 Melakarta Rāgas — the complete system of parent scales that organizes the entire melodic universe of Carnatic music

285
From the Eternal to the Expressed

  1. The Sanskrit literary-philosophical tradition — specifically the compositions of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri and the metaphorical-devotional literature of Śaṅkarācārya

These three domains are not, in truth, separate. They are three facets of a single diamond — three expressions of the one reality that the tradition calls Shabda Brahman (the Absolute as Sound) or Nāda Brahman (the Absolute as Vibration). The 22 Śrutis are the atoms of this sonic absolute. The 72 Melakartas are its molecules. The Sanskrit language — in its mantric, musical, and philosophical expressions — is its living body.

II. The Threefold Healing Proposition

The central proposition of this work can be stated in three parts:

First: The 22 Śrutis of Indian music are not merely acoustic curiosities or theoretical abstractions. Each Śruti represents a specific frequency relationship that produces a specific physiological, psychological, and spiritual effect upon the human organism. The 22 Śrutis collectively constitute a complete pharmacopoeia of sound — a set of 22 distinct vibrational medicines, each with its own therapeutic profile.

Second: The 72 Melakarta Rāgas are not merely a convenient classification of scales. Each Melakarta represents a specific combination of Śruti material that creates a unique therapeutic field — a specific pattern of vibrational energies that, when sustained through musical performance, reorganizes the listener's consciousness at every level. The 72 Melakartas collectively constitute a complete melodic formulary — a set of 72 distinct therapeutic interventions, systematically organized to cover the entire range of human psychological and spiritual possibility.

Third: The Sanskrit language — as employed in the kṛtis of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri and in the philosophical literature of Śaṅkarācārya — is not merely a medium of communication or devotional expression. It is a vibrational healing instrument — a language whose very phonemes activate specific body regions, whose compound sounds create complex resonance patterns, and whose meanings convey the transformative truths of Advaita Vedānta that heal at the deepest level of the soul.

When these three elements converge — when a Dīkṣitar kṛti is performed with correct Śruti intonation in the appropriate Melakarta Rāga, with full attention to the Sanskrit

286
PREFACE

phonemes and their meanings, and with genuine Bhakti (devotion) — the result is complete healing: a therapeutic intervention that addresses the physical body through vibrational frequency, the emotional mind through melodic beauty and devotional content, and the spiritual soul through the direct transmission of Self-knowledge.

III. Personal Perspective

I wish to be transparent about the nature of this work and the perspective from which it is written.

This is not a work of pure musicology, though it draws heavily on musicological sources. It is not a work of pure philosophy, though it engages deeply with Vedāntic and Tantric thought. It is not a work of pure medical science, though it proposes specific therapeutic protocols and engages with contemporary neuroscience and psychoacoustics.

It is, rather, a work of integration — an attempt to reunite domains of knowledge that the modern world has fragmented but that the ancient Indian tradition understood as inseparable. In the Vedic world, the musician was a healer, the healer was a philosopher, and the philosopher was a musician. The ṛṣi who heard the Veda was simultaneously a poet, a scientist, a priest, and a physician. There was no boundary between saṅgīta (music), cikitsā (medicine), darśana (philosophy), and upāsanā (worship) — because all four were expressions of the one Shabda Brahman.

I have tried to recover something of this integral vision. Individual perceptions vary, and I acknowledge freely that what I present here is one perspective — my perspective — informed by decades of engagement with Indian classical music, Sanskrit literature, Vedāntic philosophy, and contemplative practice, as well as a sincere attempt to understand what modern science can and cannot contribute to these ancient understandings.

Where I make specific therapeutic claims — "Rāga X is beneficial for Condition Y" — I am drawing on the traditional Rāga Cikitsā literature, supplemented by what modern psychoacoustic and neuroscientific research has been able to confirm. I do not claim that these prescriptions have been validated by randomized controlled trials (most have not). I do claim that they are grounded in a coherent theoretical framework, supported by centuries of empirical observation within the tradition, and consistent with what we currently know about the effects of sound on the human organism.

287
From the Eternal to the Expressed

I also wish to acknowledge the deeply personal dimension of this work. The understanding that sound heals is not, for me, merely an intellectual proposition. It is a lived reality — a reality I have experienced in my own body, my own mind, and my own soul through decades of practice. When I describe the healing power of Rāga Tōḍi or the transformative effect of chanting the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, I am not reporting what I have read in books. I am reporting what I have experienced in my own life — and what I have witnessed in the lives of others.

This personal dimension is, I believe, a strength rather than a weakness. The Indian tradition has always understood that knowledge of sound is not merely theoretical but experiential — it must be known through the body, not merely through the mind. A musicologist who has never sung a rāga, a philosopher who has never chanted a mantra, a physician who has never experienced the healing touch of Sanskrit on their own suffering — these are, from the traditional perspective, incomplete knowers. They may understand the map, but they have not walked the territory.

I have walked some of this territory. Not all of it — the territory is infinite, and a human life is finite. But enough to know that the healing is real, that the tradition is trustworthy, and that the synthesis I attempt in this work is not merely academically interesting but practically urgent.

IV. Intended Audience

This work is written for:

  1. Musicians — particularly Carnatic musicians — who wish to deepen their understanding of the therapeutic dimensions of their art and to approach their practice not merely as aesthetic expression but as healing service.

  2. Sanskrit scholars — who wish to understand the vibrational and therapeutic properties of the language they study, and to see how these properties are activated in the compositions of Dīkṣitar, Śyāma Śāstri, and Śaṅkarācārya.

  3. Āyurvedic practitioners — who wish to integrate Rāga Cikitsā (music therapy) and Mantra Cikitsā (mantra therapy) into their clinical practice.

  4. Yoga practitioners and teachers — who wish to understand the relationship between Nāda Yoga (the yoga of sound), Mantra Yoga (the yoga of sacred formula), and the broader healing traditions of Indian music and philosophy.

288
PREFACE

  1. Medical professionals — particularly those in neurology, psychiatry, and integrative medicine — who wish to understand the traditional Indian framework for sound-based healing and to consider its implications for contemporary clinical practice.

  2. Philosophers and theologians — who wish to explore the relationship between sound, meaning, consciousness, and the absolute as understood in the Indian tradition.

  3. Anyone who has been touched by Indian music — anyone who has experienced the mysterious, inexplicable, undeniable power of a rāga to transform their state of being — and who wishes to understand WHY this happens and HOW it can be harnessed for healing.

V. A Note on Transliteration and Terminology

Sanskrit terms are transliterated according to the standard IAST (International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration) system throughout this work. Diacritical marks are used consistently to ensure accurate pronunciation — a matter of particular importance in a work that argues for the therapeutic significance of precise phonemic values.

Key terminology is defined at first occurrence and in the comprehensive glossary (Appendix A). Musical terminology follows the conventions of the Carnatic tradition. Philosophical terminology follows the conventions of the Advaita Vedānta tradition as established by Śaṅkarācārya.

VI. Acknowledgments

This work would not have been possible without the grace of the Goddess Sarasvatī, who dwells in every sound and every silence; without the lineage of gurus who have preserved and transmitted the knowledge of Nāda Brahman across millennia; without the compositions of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri, which are not merely studied but lived; without the philosophical clarity of Śaṅkarācārya, whose words are medicine for the soul; and without the countless musicians, scholars, and healers — named and unnamed — whose cumulative wisdom forms the foundation upon which this work is built.

289
From the Eternal to the Expressed

I offer this work at the feet of the Guru — the silent teacher who dwells in the cave of every heart — with the prayer that it may be of some service to those who suffer and to those who seek to heal.

OṂ Sarasvatyai Namaḥ OṂ Gurubhyo Namaḥ OṂ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

COMPREHENSIVE SUMMARY

Pages xxi–xl

Overall Summary of the Work

This treatise presents a comprehensive, integrated study of the 72 Melakarta Rāga system and the 22 Śruti system of Indian classical music, cross-referenced with the sacred musical compositions of Muttuswāmi Dīkṣitar (1775–1835) and Śyāma Śāstri (1762–1827) — two of the three great masters of the Carnatic "Trinity" — and with the philosophical and devotional literature of Ādi Śaṅkarācārya (788–820 CE), the supreme exponent of Advaita Vedānta.

The work argues that these three elements — the microtonal structure of Indian music (Śrutis), its melodic organization (Melakartas), and its textual-philosophical dimension (Sanskrit sāhitya and Vedāntic literature) — together constitute a complete system of healing for the human body, mind, and soul. This system is grounded in the vibrational properties of the Sanskrit language, activated through the devotional practice of musical performance, and illuminated by the philosophical recognition that the individual self (Ātman) is identical with the universal Self (Brahman).

The work is organized into five sections of fifty pages each (250 pages total), progressing from theoretical foundations through detailed analysis of the Śrutis and Melakartas, through examination of specific compositions and philosophical texts, to practical therapeutic protocols and clinical applications.

290
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX (Pages 1–50)

Section-by-Section Summary

SECTION I: FOUNDATIONS — THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX (Pages 1–50)

Purpose: To establish the theoretical, historical, and philosophical foundations for understanding how the 22 Śrutis, the 72 Melakartas, and the Sanskrit language function together as a healing system.

Key Arguments:

  • Sound is not merely a medium of communication but a direct therapeutic agent operating on the physical, emotional, and spiritual levels of the human being

  • The 22 Śrutis are a pharmacopoeia of microtonal frequencies, each with distinct physiological and psychological effects

  • The 72 Melakarta system is a mathematically complete organization of all possible melodic material within the Indian octave

  • Sanskrit's phonemic structure makes it uniquely suited for vibrational healing

  • Dīkṣitar's and Śyāma Śāstri's compositions are precisely designed therapeutic instruments integrating rāga, mantra, and devotion

  • Śaṅkarācārya's philosophical literature provides the ultimate context for understanding healing as Self-recognition

Key Frameworks Established:

  • The three-body model (Sthūla, Sūkṣma, Kāraṇa) and its three corresponding healing modalities

  • The five-kośa model and its correspondence with the five elements of musical healing (Śruti, Tāla, Rāga, Sāhitya, Bhakti)

  • The Rāga Cikitsā tradition and its contemporary relevance

  • The Doṣa-Rāga correspondence system

291
From the Eternal to the Expressed

SECTION II: THE 22 ŚRUTIS — THE MICROTONAL ANATOMY OF HEALING SOUND (Pages 51–100)

Purpose: To provide a complete analysis of each of the 22 Śrutis — its name, its mathematical ratio, its position within the saptasvaras, its emotional quality, and its specific healing properties — and to demonstrate how Dīkṣitar, Śyāma Śāstri, and Śaṅkarācārya employ these microtonal values in their works.

Key Arguments:

  • The 22 Śrutis are distributed asymmetrically among the seven svaras (4-3-2-4-4-3-2), creating a hierarchical system of tonal stability and flexibility

  • Each Śruti has a Sanskrit name that encodes its emotional-therapeutic quality (e.g., Dayāvatī = "compassionate," Krodhā = "fierce," Mārjanī = "purifying")

  • The mathematical ratios of the Śrutis reflect both Pythagorean (cyclical) and harmonic (just intonation) principles, providing the performer with a rich palette of therapeutic tonal colors

  • Dīkṣitar's compositions demonstrate extraordinary Śruti precision, aligning Sanskrit phonemic weight with tonal weight for maximum healing effect

  • Śyāma Śāstri's compositions specialize in "weeping intervals" — specific Śruti combinations that facilitate emotional catharsis

  • The Saundaryalaharī's 100 verses can be understood as 100 "Śrutis of beauty" — 100 microtonal inflections of the single, infinite beauty of the Goddess

292
THE COMPLETE MELODIC HEALING SYSTEM (Pages 101–150)

SECTION III: THE 72 MELAKARTA RĀGAS — THE COMPLETE MELODIC HEALING SYSTEM (Pages 101–150)

Purpose: To present a complete analysis of all 72 Melakarta Rāgas, organized into 12 Chakra groups, with specific attention to each Melakarta's therapeutic profile and its employment in the compositions of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri.

Key Arguments:

  • The 72 Melakartas arise from the systematic permutation of variable svaras (Re, Ga, Ma, Dha, Ni) within the framework of fixed svaras (Sa, Pa), producing 36 Śuddha Madhyama and 36 Prati Madhyama scales

  • The 12 Chakra groups represent 12 fundamental therapeutic modalities, progressing from deep rest (Chakra I: Indu) to maximum transcendence (Chakra XII: Āditya)

  • The Prati Madhyama Melakartas (37–72) introduce transformative, pattern-breaking energies that are essential for deep healing

  • Dīkṣitar's Kāmalāmbā Navāvaraṇa cycle constitutes a complete nine-stage healing protocol mapped onto the Śrī Cakra

  • Śyāma Śāstri's concentrated use of a few rāgas (especially Ānandabhairavī) demonstrates the depth that is possible when a healer specializes rather than generalizes

  • The 72 Melakartas collectively represent a complete map of human consciousness — 72 possible modes of experiencing reality

293
From the Eternal to the Expressed

SECTION IV: DĪKṢITAR, ŚYĀMA ŚĀSTRI, AND ŚAṄKARĀCĀRYA — THE HEALING TEXTS (Pages 151–200)

Purpose: To examine in detail the specific compositions and texts that constitute the primary healing repertoire — Dīkṣitar's Navagraha, Navāvaraṇa, and Pañcabhūta/Pañcaliṅga cycles; Śyāma Śāstri's devotional kṛtis, svarājatis, and varṇams; and Śaṅkarācārya's Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, Ātmabodha, Bhaja Govindam, Saundaryalaharī, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotram.

Key Arguments:

  • Dīkṣitar was a mantravādin (wielder of sacred formulae) whose compositions are mantra-structures designed to activate specific cosmic energies

  • The Navagraha Kṛtis provide targeted astrological-musical remedies for specific planetary afflictions

  • The Kāmalāmbā Navāvaraṇa Kṛtis constitute a complete Śrī Vidyā healing journey through nine stages of consciousness

  • Śyāma Śāstri models healthy attachment to the Divine Feminine, providing emotional healing through the therapeutic relationship with the Goddess

  • His svarājatis and varṇams create therapeutic oscillation between pure sound (Nāda) and meaningful text (Shabda)

  • Śaṅkarācārya's texts provide the diagnosis (avidyā as the root disease), the treatment (viveka as the discriminating medicine), and the cure (Ātma-jñāna as Self-recognition)

  • The Saundaryalaharī is the supreme synthesis of mantra, yantra, and devotion — each verse functioning as a complete healing intervention

294
THE HEALING TOUCH OF SANSKRIT SOUND (Pages 201–250)

SECTION V: SYNTHESIS — THE HEALING TOUCH OF SANSKRIT SOUND (Pages 201–250)

Purpose: To bring all elements together in a practical synthesis — providing specific phonemic healing protocols, body-mind-soul healing models, rāga-by-rāga therapeutic protocols, clinical case studies, and a vision for an integrated science of Nāda Medicine.

Key Arguments:

  • Six specific phonemic healing protocols (for throat/thyroid, respiratory, cardiac, neurological, hormonal, and emotional conditions) demonstrate how Sanskrit sounds target specific body systems

  • A comprehensive Rāga-Body Map correlates specific Melakartas with specific body systems, integrating Āyurvedic doṣa theory

  • Three detailed rāga-specific healing protocols (Tōḍi for grief, Kalyāṇi for depression, Śaṅkarābharaṇam for general wellness) provide step-by-step clinical procedures

  • Three clinical case studies (chronic anxiety, post-bereavement depression, chronic pain with spiritual crisis) demonstrate the application of the system to real-world conditions

  • Bhakti (devotion) is identified as the essential catalyst without which all techniques remain merely techniques

  • A daily, weekly, and seasonal practice framework integrates all elements into a sustainable healing lifestyle

  • The ultimate healing is the recognition of the Self as Brahman — the silence from which all sound arises and to which all sound returns

295
From the Eternal to the Expressed

Chapter 1.1: Introduction to Shabda Brahman: The Eternal Word

Pages 1–5

The concept of Shabda Brahman represents one of the most profound and far-reaching philosophical propositions in the entire corpus of Indian thought. It is, at its essence, the assertion that the ultimate reality — Brahman, the absolute, the infinite ground of all existence — is not merely silent, formless, and abstract, but is fundamentally constituted by, and accessible through, sound. Not ordinary sound, not the casual noise of the material world, but a primordial, self-existent, eternal vibration that is simultaneously the substance and the intelligence of all creation.

This idea did not emerge in isolation. It arose from millennia of contemplative inquiry, ritualistic precision, and experiential verification conducted by the ṛṣis (seers) of the Vedic tradition. When the Ṛg Veda declares "Prajāpati vai idam āsīt" — in the beginning was Prajāpati, the lord of creation — and goes on to describe how creation proceeded from his word (vāc), it establishes the foundational axiom that sound precedes matter, that vibration precedes form, that the word is ontologically prior to the world.

The term "Shabda Brahman" (शब्द ब्रह्मन्) is a tatpuruṣa compound, literally meaning "the Brahman that is Word" or "the Absolute as Sound." It appears across multiple textual traditions:

  • In the Vedas, particularly in the hymns to Vāc (Speech), where the goddess of speech is identified with the creative power of the universe

  • In the Upaniṣads, where the syllable OṂ is described as the sonic essence of Brahman

346
THE METAPHYSICS OF PRIMORDIAL SOUND

  • In the Vyākaraṇa (grammatical) tradition, particularly in Bhartṛhari's Vākyapadīya, where Shabda Brahman is the ultimate reality from which all language, meaning, and existence emanate

  • In the Tantric traditions, where the Mātṛkā (the divine alphabet) is understood as the body of the goddess, each letter a living power

  • In the Saṅgīta Śāstra (musicological) tradition, where Nāda Brahman — the Absolute as musical sound — is the governing principle of all rāga, tāla, and svara

The present work undertakes an ambitious synthesis. It seeks to demonstrate that three apparently distinct domains — the 52 Mātṛkā letters of the Sanskrit alphabet, the 72 Melakarta Rāgas of the Carnatic musical system, and the 22 Śrutis (microtonal intervals) of Indian acoustics — are not three separate subjects but three facets of a single, unified reality: Shabda Brahman.

The Fundamental Proposition

The central argument of this treatise can be stated simply: All structured sound is a manifestation of Brahman, and the various systems by which human beings have mapped, classified, and organized sound are windows into the architecture of consciousness itself.

This is not merely a poetic or metaphorical claim. The Sanskrit alphabet is not an arbitrary collection of symbols. Each of its 52 letters (in the expanded Tāntric enumeration) corresponds to a specific point of articulation in the human vocal apparatus, a specific energetic center in the subtle body, a specific planetary influence in the cosmos, and a specific aspect of divine consciousness. When these letters are ritually installed upon the body through the practice of Mātṛkā Nyāsa, they do not merely "symbolize" the divine — they activate the vibrational pattern of divinity within the practitioner's own being.

Similarly, the 72 Melakarta system is not merely a convenient classification of musical scales. It represents the complete set of possible harmonic relationships between the seven fundamental tones (saptasvaras), which are themselves sonic manifestations of the same primordial energies expressed in the Mātṛkā. The mathematical precision of this system — based on the permutation of specific intervals in the lower and upper tetrachords —

347
From the Eternal to the Expressed

mirrors the mathematical precision of the cosmos itself.

And the 22 Śrutis are not merely an acoustic curiosity. They represent the finest possible discriminations of pitch that the human ear and voice can reliably produce and perceive, and they form the microtonal substrate upon which all Indian music — and, by extension, all Indian sacred sound — is constructed.

The Experiential Dimension

It is crucial to emphasize from the outset that Shabda Brahman is not purely a theoretical construct. It is, above all, an experiential reality. The Vedic seers did not arrive at their understanding of sound through abstract speculation. They arrived at it through direct, sustained, disciplined engagement with sound — through the chanting of mantras, the performance of Vedic rituals, the practice of prāṇāyāma (breath control), and the cultivation of deep meditative states in which the subtlest levels of sonic vibration became directly perceptible.

This experiential dimension is preserved in the living traditions of:

  • Mantra Śāstra — the science of sacred formulae

  • Nāda Yoga — the yoga of inner sound

  • Svara Śāstra — the science of musical tone

  • Tantra — the technology of consciousness transformation through sound, form, and energy

In each of these traditions, the practitioner is not a passive observer of sound but an active participant in its creation, modulation, and internalization. The body becomes an instrument. The breath becomes a medium. Consciousness becomes both the performer and the audience.

The Medical and Psychological Imperative

As the author of this work has observed — and this point deserves special emphasis — the understanding of Shabda Brahman has direct and urgent relevance for medical science, particularly in the domains of physiology and psychology.

The human brain does not merely "hear" sound. It is organized by sound. The auditory cortex, the Broca's and Wernicke's areas, the limbic system, the prefrontal cortex — all of these are shaped by, and responsive to, specific patterns of sound. The phenomenon

348
THE METAPHYSICS OF PRIMORDIAL SOUND

of psychosis, in which the normal processing of sensory information becomes disordered, can be understood, from the perspective of Nāda Upāsanā, as a fundamental disruption in the relationship between consciousness and its sonic substrate.

This is not to suggest that chanting mantras is a replacement for psychiatric medication. It is to suggest, however, that the ancient Indian understanding of how sound moves through the four stages of manifestation — from the silent potentiality of Parā, through the visionary apprehension of Paśyantī, through the mental formulation of Madhyamā, to the physical utterance of Vaikharī — provides a map of consciousness that is at least as sophisticated as, and potentially more comprehensive than, current neuroscientific models.

The four upper chakras — Anāhata (heart), Viśuddha (throat), Ājñā (third eye), and Sahasrāra (crown) — correspond precisely to this four-stage journey of sound. The impulse arises in the heart (Anāhata, the "unstruck sound"), takes form in the throat (Viśuddha, the center of purification and expression), achieves focused intentionality between the eyebrows (Ājñā, the command center), and finally dissolves into transcendent awareness at the crown (Sahasrāra, the thousand-petaled lotus).

Medical science, particularly neurology and psychiatry, stands to gain enormously from a serious engagement with this model. The mechanisms by which specific sound frequencies affect brainwave patterns, autonomic nervous system function, hormonal secretion, and emotional regulation are only beginning to be understood by modern science. The Indian tradition has been mapping these mechanisms for thousands of years.

Scope and Structure of This Work

This work is divided into five major sections:

Section I (the present section) establishes the metaphysical, philosophical, and experiential foundations of Shabda Brahman. It traces the concept through the Vedic, Upaniṣadic, grammatical, and Tantric traditions, and establishes the theoretical framework within which the subsequent sections will operate.

Section II provides a detailed examination of the 52 Mātṛkā letters and the practice of Mātṛkā Nyāsa. It explores each letter in terms of its phonetic properties, its energetic correspondences, its planetary associations, and its role in mantra construction. Special

349
From the Eternal to the Expressed

attention is given to the bījākṣaras (seed syllables) and their composite structure.

Section III examines the 72 Melakarta Rāga system as a musical manifestation of Shabda Brahman. It explores the mathematical structure of the system, the correspondence between svaras and Mātṛkā letters, and the therapeutic potential of specific rāgas.

Section IV investigates the 22 Śrutis — the microtonal intervals that form the acoustic foundation of Indian music. It examines their mathematical ratios, their perceptual properties, their relationship to both the Mātṛkā and the Melakarta systems, and their significance for sound-based healing.

Section V brings all three systems together in a comprehensive synthesis, with special emphasis on the medical, physiological, and psychological implications. It proposes a framework for integrating the ancient understanding of Shabda Brahman with contemporary neuroscience, psychoacoustics, and therapeutic practice.

Throughout, the work maintains fidelity to the traditional sources while remaining open to dialogue with modern science. Individual perceptions vary, as the author has wisely noted. This work does not claim to present the final truth about the nature of sound and consciousness. It claims only to present one coherent, deeply informed, and experientially grounded perspective — one that deserves serious consideration from scholars, practitioners, and scientists alike.

Chapter 1.2: The Vedic Origins of Sound Theology

Pages 6–10

The roots of Shabda Brahman lie deep in the soil of Vedic revelation. To understand this concept fully, we must return to the earliest stratum of Indian sacred literature — the Saṃhitās, particularly the Ṛg Veda — and trace the gradual unfolding of the idea that sound is not merely a medium of communication but the very fabric of reality.

Vāc Sūkta: The Hymn of Speech

The most celebrated Vedic text on the nature of sound is the Vāc Sūkta (Ṛg Veda 10.125), also known as the Devī Sūkta, in which the goddess Vāc (Speech) proclaims her own cosmic sovereignty:

350
THE METAPHYSICS OF PRIMORDIAL SOUND

"I move with the Rudras, with the Vasus, with the Ādityas and with the Viśvedevas. I support both Mitra and Varuṇa, both Indra and Agni, and both the Aśvins. I support the swelling Soma, and Tvaṣṭṛ, and Pūṣan, and Bhaga. I bestow wealth on the one who offers oblation, who presses Soma, and who worships with devotion. I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures, the most thoughtful, the first of those who deserve worship. The gods have placed me in many places, with many homes to enter and to dwell in. Through me alone, all eat the food they eat — those who see, those who breathe, those who hear what is spoken. Though they do not realize it, they dwell in me. Hear, O celebrated one, the truth of what I tell you. I, verily, myself announce and utter the word that gods and humans alike rejoice in. Whom I love, that one I make mighty; I make that one a ṛṣi, a sage, a knower of Brahman. I stretch the bow for Rudra, that his arrow may strike and slay the hater of devotion. I rouse and direct the battle for the people. I have pervaded both Heaven and Earth. I give birth to the Father on the head of this world. My womb is in the waters, in the ocean. From there I spread through all beings and touch the very sky with the crown of my head. I breathe forth like the wind, clasping all beings. Beyond the sky, beyond this earth — so vast have I become in my greatness."

This extraordinary hymn establishes several foundational principles:

  1. Vāc is omnipresent and omnipotent. She moves with all classes of deities; she supports the fundamental cosmic powers (Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Agni). Sound is not a secondary phenomenon but a primary cosmic force.

  2. Vāc is the sustainer of all life. "Through me alone, all eat the food they eat." Every living being participates in the reality of sound, whether consciously or unconsciously.

  3. Vāc is the maker of sages. "Whom I love, that one I make a ṛṣi, a knower of Brahman." The capacity for spiritual realization is itself a gift of sound — a function of one's relationship with the vibrational ground of being.

  4. Vāc is cosmogonic. "I give birth to the Father on the head of this world." Sound precedes even the creator. It is the matrix from which creation itself emerges.

  5. Vāc is infinite. "Beyond the sky, beyond this earth — so vast have I become." Sound is not limited to the physical realm. It extends beyond all spatial and temporal boundaries.

351
From the Eternal to the Expressed

The Prātiśākhyas and the Science of Phonetics

While the Saṃhitā hymns provide the theological foundation for Shabda Brahman, the Prātiśākhyas — ancient phonetic treatises attached to the various Vedic schools — provide the empirical foundation. These texts, composed perhaps as early as 800 BCE, represent the world's first systematic works on phonetics and phonology.

The Prātiśākhyas classify every sound of the Vedic language according to:

  • Sthāna (place of articulation): kaṇṭhya (guttural/throat), tālavya (palatal), mūrdhanya (cerebral/retroflex), dantya (dental), oṣṭhya (labial)

  • Prayatna (effort of articulation): spṛṣṭa (fully closed), īṣat-spṛṣṭa (slightly closed), vivṛta (open), saṃvṛta (closed)

  • Karaṇa (articulatory organ): jihvāmūla (tongue root), jihvāmadhya (tongue middle), jihvāgra (tongue tip), adhara (lower lip), etc.

  • Prāṇa (breath involvement): mahāprāṇa (aspirated), alpaprāṇa (unaspirated)

  • Nāda (sonority): ghoṣavat (voiced), aghoṣa (unvoiced)

This extraordinary precision of classification was not merely linguistic. It served a ritual purpose: the correct pronunciation of every Vedic syllable was considered essential for the efficacy of the yajña (sacrifice). A mispronounced mantra was not merely aesthetically deficient — it was ritually dangerous. The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa warns: "The word wrongly pronounced does not achieve its purpose. It becomes like a thunderbolt turned against the speaker."

This insistence on phonetic precision reflects a deep conviction that the sounds of the Vedic language are not arbitrary signs but natural, inherent expressions of the realities they denote. The word is not a symbol of the thing — the word IS the thing, at the level of sonic reality. This is the essence of the doctrine of Shabda Brahman.

Praṇava: OṂ as the Sonic Essence of Brahman

No discussion of Vedic sound theology can proceed without extended consideration of the syllable OṂ (also written AUM or Praṇava). This syllable occupies a unique position in Indian thought: it is simultaneously the shortest possible mantra and the most comprehensive possible expression of ultimate reality.

352
THE METAPHYSICS OF PRIMORDIAL SOUND

The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, perhaps the most concentrated of all Upaniṣadic texts, devotes its entire twelve verses to an analysis of OṂ:

"OṂ — this syllable is all this. What has been, what is, and what shall be — all this is the syllable OṂ. And whatever else there is beyond the three times — that too is the syllable OṂ."

The Māṇḍūkya proceeds to analyze OṂ into its component sounds:

  • A (the first vowel) corresponds to the waking state (jāgrat), the gross body (sthūla śarīra), and the experience of the external world. It represents Vaiśvānara, the universal person as experienced in everyday consciousness.

  • U (the second element) corresponds to the dream state (svapna), the subtle body (sūkṣma śarīra), and the experience of the internal mental world. It represents Taijasa, the luminous inner self.

  • M (the third element) corresponds to deep sleep (suṣupti), the causal body (kāraṇa śarīra), and the experience of undifferentiated awareness. It represents Prājña, the wise one who knows from the depth of dreamless sleep.

  • The silence that follows (amātra, the "measureless") corresponds to Turīya, the fourth state — pure consciousness itself, beyond all states, beyond all distinction, the absolute ground of being.

This analysis is of immense significance for our study because it demonstrates that the structure of a single syllable — OṂ — mirrors the entire structure of consciousness and reality. The universe, the self, and the syllable are isomorphic. They share the same architecture, the same sequence of manifestation, the same fundamental patterns.

When we later come to examine the Bījākṣaras (OṂ, AIM, HRĪṂ, ŚRĪṂ, KLĪṂ), we will see that each of them contains this same triadic structure — a vowel component (the energetic core), a consonantal component (the structural framework), and a nasal/anusvāra component (the resonant dissolution) — and that this structure recapitulates in miniature the entire process by which Shabda Brahman manifests as the created world.

353
From the Eternal to the Expressed

The Concept of Ṛta: Cosmic Order as Sonic Pattern

Another crucial Vedic concept for understanding Shabda Brahman is Ṛta — the cosmic order, the fundamental pattern or rhythm of reality. Ṛta is not a law imposed upon the universe from outside. It is the intrinsic pattern of the universe itself — the way things naturally are when they are in harmony with their own essential nature.

The connection between Ṛta and sound is intimate. The Vedic rituals, which were understood as means of maintaining and restoring Ṛta, were primarily sonic events. The chanting of mantras, the singing of Sāma, the precise recitation of Yajus formulae — all of these were understood not as petitions to distant gods but as participatory acts of cosmic maintenance. By producing the right sounds in the right sequence at the right time, the Vedic priests were tuning the world, keeping the cosmic instrument in harmony.

This concept will prove essential when we come to examine the 72 Melakarta Rāgas. Each rāga is not merely a scale or a melodic pattern but a specific expression of Ṛta — a particular pattern of sonic order that has the power to evoke, sustain, and transform specific states of consciousness and being. The ancient association of specific rāgas with specific times of day, seasons of the year, and emotional states reflects this Ṛta-consciousness: the recognition that sound and cosmic order are inseparable.

Sāma Veda: The Vedic Foundation of Music

If the Ṛg Veda provides the theological foundation of Shabda Brahman and the Prātiśākhyas provide the phonetic foundation, the Sāma Veda provides the musical foundation. The Sāma Veda is, in essence, the Ṛg Veda set to music — its mantras arranged and notated for melodic chanting.

The Sāma Veda employs a system of seven tones (saptasvaras), notated by numerals (1 through 7), which correspond to the seven notes of the Indian musical scale:

Sāma Tone Musical Svara Name
1 (Pradhama) Ma Madhyama
2 (Dvitīya) Ga Gāndhāra
3 (Tṛtīya) Re Ṛṣabha
