Chapter 1.1: Introduction: The Triune Healing — Sound, Meaning, and Silence

Pages 1–6

There exists in the Indian tradition a profound and ancient understanding that has no precise equivalent in modern Western thought: the understanding that sound, when correctly structured, correctly intoned, and correctly understood, heals. Not merely as a pleasant distraction from suffering, not merely as a psychological palliative, but as a direct, material, transformative intervention upon the physical body, the emotional mind, and the spiritual core of the human being.

This understanding rests upon three pillars:

1. Śruti (the microtonal interval) — the precise, mathematically defined frequency relationship between two tones. The 22 Śrutis of Indian music represent the complete spectrum of vibrational possibilities within a single octave. Each Śruti produces a specific physiological and psychological effect. The 22 Śrutis are, in effect, a pharmacopoeia of pure sound — 22 distinct "medicines" that operate directly upon the nervous system, the endocrine system, and the subtle energy body.

2. Rāga (the melodic mode) — the organized, aesthetically shaped, emotionally charged arrangement of Śrutis into a coherent musical personality. The 72 Melakarta Rāgas of the Carnatic system represent the complete set of possible melodic medicines — 72 distinct combinations of tonal material, each with its own therapeutic profile, its own emotional signature, its own spiritual resonance. When a Melakarta Rāga is performed with skill, devotion, and understanding, it does not merely please the ear — it reorganizes the listener's consciousness.

3. Sāhitya (the Sanskrit text) — the meaningful words that are married to the melody. In the kṛtis of the great Carnatic composers — particularly Muttuswāmi Dīkṣitar (1775–1835) and Śyāma Śāstri (1762–1827), two of the "Trinity" of Carnatic music —

401
From the Eternal to the Expressed

the Sanskrit text is not merely a vehicle for conveying devotional sentiment. It is a mantra — a precisely constructed arrangement of Sanskrit phonemes that activates specific energetic centers in the singer and the listener. Each word is chosen not only for its meaning but for its sound — for its phonetic properties, its vibrational qualities, its capacity to resonate with specific chakras, nāḍīs, and prāṇic pathways.

When these three elements — Śruti, Rāga, and Sāhitya — converge in a single performance, the result is not merely beautiful music. It is healing in the deepest sense — a restoration of harmony at every level of the human being.

The philosophical foundation for this healing is provided by the Advaita Vedānta of Ādi Śaṅkarācārya (788–820 CE), whose metaphorical and devotional literature — the Bhaja Govindam, the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, the Ātmabodha, the Saundaryalaharī, the Śivānandalaharī, the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotram, and many others — provides the conceptual medicine that completes the sonic medicine of the composers. Śaṅkarācārya's texts, composed in exquisite Sanskrit verse, employ metaphor, paradox, and devotional intensity to effect a fundamental shift in the listener's self-understanding — from identification with the suffering, limited ego to recognition of the infinite, blissful Self (Ātman) that is identical with Brahman.

The Three Bodies and Their Three Medicines

The Indian tradition recognizes three bodies (śarīras) that constitute the human being:

  1. Sthūla Śarīra (the gross/physical body) — made of the five elements (earth, water, fire, air, space), sustained by food, subject to disease, aging, and death.

  2. Sūkṣma Śarīra (the subtle body) — made of the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and the five prāṇas; the seat of thoughts, emotions, memories, and dreams.

  3. Kāraṇa Śarīra (the causal body) — the seed-form of the individual, containing the vāsanās (latent tendencies) and saṃskāras (karmic impressions) that determine the shape of future births. This is the level of the soul (jīva) in its deepest, most essential nature.

Each of these bodies has its own form of illness and its own form of healing:

402
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX
Body Illness Healing Agent Musical Correspondence
Sthūla (Physical) Disease (roga) Āyurvedic medicine + Rāga Cikitsā Śruti (microtonal frequency)
Sūkṣma (Subtle/Mental) Affliction (kleśa) Mantra + Bhakti + Rāga Rāga (melodic mode)
Kāraṇa (Causal/Soul) Ignorance (avidyā) Jñāna (knowledge) + Vedāntic realization Sāhitya (Sanskrit meaning)

The kṛtis of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri operate on all three levels simultaneously:

  • At the physical level, the specific Śruti values of the rāga, the precise intonation of each note, creates vibratory patterns that directly affect the body's nervous and endocrine systems.

  • At the mental/emotional level, the rāga's aesthetic personality (rasa) — its mood, its associations, its characteristic movements — reshapes the listener's emotional landscape, dissolving negative patterns and establishing positive ones.

  • At the soul level, the Sanskrit sāhitya — the meaningful text — conveys Vedāntic truths that, when deeply absorbed, uproot the fundamental ignorance (avidyā) that is the root cause of all suffering.

Śaṅkarācārya's literature operates primarily at the third level — the level of the soul — but it does so through Sanskrit language that is itself sonically potent, and through metaphors drawn from the world of nature and the body that resonate at the physical and emotional levels as well.

The Composer-Philosopher Continuum

It is no accident that Dīkṣitar, Śyāma Śāstri, and Śaṅkarācārya share certain fundamental characteristics:

  1. All three are steeped in Sanskrit. Dīkṣitar composed almost exclusively in Sanskrit (unlike his contemporary Tyāgarāja, who preferred Telugu). Śyāma Śāstri composed primarily in Telugu but with heavy Sanskrit influence and several pure Sanskrit compositions. Śaṅkarācārya's entire literary output is in Sanskrit.

403
From the Eternal to the Expressed

  1. All three are devoted to the Goddess. Dīkṣitar's primary deity is the Goddess in her various forms (Kāmalāmbā, Mīnākṣī, Annapūrṇā, etc.). Śyāma Śāstri's primary deity is the Goddess Kāmākṣī at Kāñcīpuram. Śaṅkarācārya, despite being an Advaitin who taught the formless Brahman, composed some of the most passionate goddess-devotion in all of Sanskrit literature (the Saundaryalaharī).

  2. All three employ sound as a means of transformation. Dīkṣitar uses the sonic properties of rāga and Sanskrit mantra. Śyāma Śāstri uses the emotional power of melody and rhythmic complexity. Śaṅkarācārya uses the vibrational and semantic properties of poetic Sanskrit.

  3. All three understand healing as a multi-level process. For Dīkṣitar, the Navagraha Kṛtis heal the planetary afflictions that cause disease. For Śyāma Śāstri, the outpouring of emotion in the presence of the Divine Mother heals the heart. For Śaṅkarācārya, the recognition of one's true nature as Brahman heals the fundamental wound of existential ignorance.

The Central Thesis

The central thesis of this work is:

The 72 Melakarta Rāgas, understood through the lens of the 22 Śrutis, and illuminated by the kṛtis of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri and the metaphorical literature of Śaṅkarācārya, constitute a complete system of healing for the body, mind, and soul — a system grounded in the vibrational properties of the Sanskrit language and activated through the practice of devotional music.

This is not a metaphorical claim. It is a claim about the actual, demonstrable effects of specific sound frequencies, specific melodic patterns, and specific Sanskrit phonemic sequences upon the human organism. The evidence for this claim comes from three sources:

  1. The traditional literature — the Nāṭyaśāstra, the Saṅgīta Ratnākara, the Svara Mela Kalānidhi, the Caturdaṇḍi Prakāśikā, and the numerous texts on mantra śāstra, Āyurveda, and yoga that describe the effects of specific sounds on the body and mind.

404
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

  1. The compositional practice — the extraordinary precision and intentionality with which Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri chose their rāgas, constructed their sāhityas, and embedded layers of healing meaning in every aspect of their compositions.

  2. The experiential testimony — the consistent reports, across centuries and cultures, of the transformative effects of Indian classical music on listeners' physical health, emotional well-being, and spiritual awareness.

Modern science is beginning to corroborate these traditional claims through research in psychoacoustics, neuroplasticity, the neuroscience of music, and the effects of specific frequencies on cellular biology. But the traditional understanding goes far deeper than anything modern science has yet explored, and it is this traditional understanding — in all its richness, precision, and subtlety — that we seek to present in this work.

Chapter 1.2: The 22 Śrutis: Anatomy of Microtonal Consciousness

Pages 7-13

What is a Śruti?

The word "Śruti" (श्रुति) comes from the root √śru, meaning "to hear." In its most general sense, Śruti means "that which is heard" — and it is used in two entirely different but related contexts in Indian tradition:

  1. Śruti as Revelation: The Vedas are called "Śruti" because they are "that which was heard" by the ṛṣis in states of deep meditation. They were not composed by human authors; they were received by human listeners from the eternal, self-existent sound of Brahman.

  2. Śruti as Microtone: In the context of music, a Śruti is the smallest interval of pitch that the trained human ear can reliably distinguish. The Indian musical tradition identifies 22 such intervals within a single octave.

The coincidence of these two meanings is not accidental. The 22 Śrutis of music are, from the traditional perspective, a form of revelation — a direct, audible manifestation of the mathematical order of the cosmos. To hear a Śruti with full awareness is, in a

405
From the Eternal to the Expressed

real sense, to hear the Veda — to receive, through the ear, a communication from the fundamental structure of reality.

The 22 Śrutis: Names and Locations

The classical enumeration of the 22 Śrutis is found in Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra (circa 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE) and is elaborated in Śārṅgadeva's Saṅgīta Ratnākara (13th century CE). The 22 Śrutis are distributed among the seven svaras as follows:

Svara Śruti Count Śruti Names Cumulative Position
Sa (Ṣaḍja) 4 Tīvrā, Kumudvatī, Mandā, Chandovatī 1, 2, 3, 4
Re (Ṛṣabha) 3 Dayāvatī, Ranjanī, Rati 5, 6, 7
Ga (Gāndhāra) 2 Raudrī, Krodhā 8, 9
Ma (Madhyama) 4 Vajrikā, Prasāriṇī, Prīti, Mārjanī 10, 11, 12, 13
Pa (Pañcama) 4 Kṣiti, Raktā, Sandīpanī, Ālāpinī 14, 15, 16, 17
Dha (Dhaivata) 3 Madantī, Rohiṇī, Ramyā 18, 19, 20
Ni (Niṣāda) 2 Ugrā, Kṣobhiṇī 21, 22
Total 22

The Distribution Pattern: 4-3-2-4-4-3-2

The asymmetric distribution of Śrutis among the seven svaras — Sa(4), Re(3), Ga(2), Ma(4), Pa(4), Dha(3), Ni(2) — is one of the most remarkable features of the Indian tonal system. It reveals several profound truths:

1. Hierarchical Stability: The svaras with 4 Śrutis (Sa, Ma, Pa) are the most stable, the most consonant, the most structurally important. Sa and Pa form the perfect fifth — the most consonant interval after the unison. Ma (the fourth) completes the fundamental tetrachord. These three tones are the "bones" of the musical skeleton.

2. Emotional Flexibility: The svaras with 3 Śrutis (Re, Dha) are moderately flexible — they can be intoned higher or lower to create different emotional shadings without losing their identity. The svaras with 2 Śrutis (Ga, Ni) are the most flexible and the most emotionally charged — they are the svaras that most powerfully distinguish one rāga from another.

406
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

3. Healing Implications: The svaras with more Śrutis (Sa, Ma, Pa) are the grounding, stabilizing, centering svaras — appropriate for calming the body and settling the nervous system. The svaras with fewer Śrutis (Ga, Ni) are the emotionally expressive, transformative svaras — appropriate for releasing blocked emotions and catalyzing psychological change.

Each of the 22 Śrutis has a name, and these names are not arbitrary. They encode the emotional and energetic quality of the microtone:

The fact that these names range from the gentle (Kumudvatī, Mandā, Dayāvatī) to the fierce (Raudrī, Krodhā, Ugrā) indicates that the 22 Śrutis encompass the full range of human emotional experience — and, by implication, the full range of therapeutic interventions. Every emotional state has its corresponding Śruti; every Śruti has its corresponding healing function.

Śruti as the Foundation of Rāga

The relationship between Śruti and Rāga is the relationship between atoms and molecules, between ingredients and recipes, between individual colors and paintings. The 22 Śrutis provide the raw tonal material; the 72 Melakarta Rāgas organize this material into specific, aesthetically meaningful, therapeutically potent configurations.

When a musician performs a Rāga, they do not merely hit the "right notes." They intone each note with a specific Śruti value — a specific microtonal placement that gives the note its characteristic color, weight, and emotional quality. The difference between a masterful performance and a mediocre one lies largely in the precision of Śruti — in the musician's ability to place each note at exactly the right microtonal location for maximum expressive and therapeutic effect.

Dīkṣitar was legendary for his Śruti awareness. His compositions are designed to showcase the specific Śruti values that characterize each rāga, and his choice of Sanskrit syllables often mirrors the Śruti movement — the phonetic weight of the syllable matching the tonal weight of the note. This phoneme-Śruti matching is one of the deepest levels of healing embedded in his compositions, and we will examine numerous examples in later chapters.

408
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

Chapter 1.3: Mathematical Framework of the 72 Melakarta System

Pages 14–20

The Logic of 72

The number 72 is not arbitrary. It arises from a precise mathematical calculation based on the systematic combination of all possible variants of the seven svaras within the constraints of the Indian melodic system.

In the Melakarta system:

  • Sa (the tonic) and Pa (the fifth) are invariable. They appear in every Melakarta in their natural positions. Sa is always at the 4th Śruti; Pa is always at the 17th Śruti.

  • Ma (the fourth) has exactly two variants:

    • Śuddha Ma (M1): The natural fourth, at the 13th Śruti

    • Prati Ma (M2): The augmented fourth, at the 14th Śruti position (actually the first Śruti of Pa's range)

  • The remaining four svaras — Re, Ga, Dha, Ni — each have three variants:

Svara Variant 1 Variant 2 Variant 3
Re Śuddha (R1) Catusśruti (R2) Ṣaṭśruti (R3)
Ga Śuddha (G1) Sādhāraṇa (G2) Antara (G3)
Dha Śuddha (D1) Catusśruti (D2) Ṣaṭśruti (D3)
Ni Śuddha (N1) Kaiśiki (N2) Kākali (N3)

The Constraint: Ascending Order

The critical constraint is that the svaras must appear in ascending order of pitch within the scale. This means that Re and Ga cannot overlap in the wrong direction — if Re takes a high variant, Ga must take an equal or higher variant. The same applies to Dha and Ni.

The possible combinations for Re-Ga (the Pūrvāṅga or lower tetrachord, along with fixed Sa and variable Ma) are:

409
From the Eternal to the Expressed
Combination Re Ga Comment
1 R1 G1 Both at lowest position
2 R1 G2 Re low, Ga middle
3 R1 G3 Re low, Ga high
4 R2 G2 Re middle, Ga middle (R2 = G1 enharmonically)
5 R2 G3 Re middle, Ga high
6 R3 G3 Both at highest position (R3 = G2 enharmonically)

6 combinations for Re-Ga.

Similarly, 6 combinations for Dha-Ni (the Uttarāṅga or upper tetrachord, along with fixed Pa).

The total for a given Ma position: 6 (Pūrvāṅga) × 6 (Uttarāṅga) = 36 Melakartas.

With two Ma positions: 36 × 2 = 72 Melakartas.

The 12 Chakra Grouping

The 72 Melakartas are traditionally organized into 12 groups of 6, called "Chakras" (not to be confused with the yoga chakras, though there are analogical connections). Each Chakra shares the same Pūrvāṅga (same Re-Ga-Ma combination) and varies only in the Uttarāṅga (Dha-Ni combination):

Chakra Re-Ga-Ma Melakarta Numbers Characteristics
I - Indu R1-G1-M1 1–6 Most natural, primordial
II - Netra R1-G2-M1 7–12 Gentle expansion
III - Agni R1-G3-M1 13–18 Bright, illuminating
IV - Veda R2-G2-M1 19–24 Balanced, wise
V - Bāṇa R2-G3-M1 25–30 Directed, powerful
VI - Ṛtu R3-G3-M1 31–36 Seasonal, cyclical
VII - Ṛṣi R1-G1-M2 37–42 Sage-like, altered
VIII - Vasu R1-G2-M2 43–48 Abundant, generous
IX - Brahma R1-G3-M2 49–54 Creative, expansive
X - Diśi R2-G2-M2 55–60 Directional, spatial
410
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX
Chakra Re-Ga-Ma Melakarta Numbers Characteristics
XI - Rudra R2-G3-M2 61–66 Fierce, transformative
XII - Āditya R3-G3-M2 67–72 Solar, transcendent

The Katapayādi System

Dīkṣitar's contemporary, Govindācārya (and the broader South Indian tradition), employed the Katapayādi numbering system to encode the Melakarta number in the first two syllables of each rāga's name. This system assigns numerical values to consonants:

Value Ka-series Ṭa-series Pa-series Ya-series
1 Ka Ṭa Pa Ya
2 Kha Ṭha Pha Ra
3 Ga Ḍa Ba La
4 Gha Ḍha Bha Va
5 Ṅa Ṇa Ma Śa
6 Ca Ta — Ṣa
7 Cha Tha — Sa
8 Ja Da — Ha
9 Jha Dha — —
0 Ña Na — —

The rule: take the first two consonants of the rāga name, find their numerical values, reverse the order, and the result is the Melakarta number.

Example: Kanakaṅgi (Melakarta 1)

  • Ka = 1, Na = 0 → reversed: 01 = 1 ✓

Example: Dhīraśaṅkarābharaṇam (Melakarta 29)

  • Dhī = 9 (Dha), Ra = 2 → reversed: 29 = 29 ✓

Example: Mecakalyāṇi (Melakarta 65)

  • Me = 5 (Ma), Ca = 6 → reversed: 65 = 65 ✓

411
From the Eternal to the Expressed

This system demonstrates the extraordinary precision of the Sanskrit-mathematical tradition. The names of the rāgas are not merely labels — they are encrypted codes that reveal the mathematical structure of the scale. This is Sanskrit functioning simultaneously as art, science, and sacred technology.

The Healing Geometry of 72

The number 72 has cosmic significance in multiple traditions:

  • 72 = 360/5: The zodiacal circle (360°) divided by the number of elements (5) yields 72. Each Melakarta thus covers 5° of the cosmic circle.

  • 72 years = approximately one degree of precessional movement of the equinoxes, linking the Melakarta cycle to the largest known astronomical cycle.

  • 72,000 nāḍīs are said to constitute the subtle body in yogic anatomy. 72 Melakartas × 1000 = 72,000, suggesting that each Melakarta governs 1000 nāḍīs.

  • 72 = 8 × 9: The product of the octave number (8, representing completion in the Sa-to-Sa cycle) and the planetary number (9, the Navagrahas), linking the Melakarta system to both musical and astrological wholeness.

These correspondences suggest that the 72 Melakarta system is not merely a convenient classification but a representation of cosmic order — a musical map of the universe that, when fully understood and fully practiced, brings the musician and the listener into alignment with that order.

Chapter 1.4: Sanskrit as a Vibrational Healing Language: Phonetics and Physiology

Pages 21–26

The Unique Properties of Sanskrit

Sanskrit (saṃskṛtam, "perfectly constructed") is not merely one language among many. It is, from the traditional Indian perspective, the language of creation — the tongue in which the Veda was revealed, the medium through which mantra operates, and the linguistic embodiment of Ṛta (cosmic order).

From a modern linguistic perspective, Sanskrit possesses several extraordinary properties that make it uniquely suited for therapeutic use:

412
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

1. Phonetic Completeness: Sanskrit utilizes virtually every possible point of articulation in the human vocal apparatus — from the glottis (Ha) to the lips (Pa), from the velum (Ka) to the teeth (Ta), from the retroflex position (Ṭa) to the palate (Ca). This means that chanting Sanskrit exercises the entire vocal mechanism, stimulating every nerve pathway associated with speech production.

2. Systematic Organization: The Sanskrit alphabet is organized according to phonetic principles (place and manner of articulation), not historical accident. This systematic organization means that moving through the alphabet — as in Mātṛkā Nyāsa or alphabetical chanting — is equivalent to performing a systematic exercise of the entire articulatory system, proceeding from the throat forward to the lips in a logical, anatomically coherent sequence.

3. Resonant Vowel System: Sanskrit's 16 vowels, including the long/short pairs and the unique syllabic consonants (Ṛ, Ḷ), create a richer resonant environment than most other languages. Chanting Sanskrit vowels activates a wider range of cranial resonances (nasal, oral, pharyngeal, and chest resonance) than chanting in languages with fewer vowel distinctions.

4. Aspiration Contrast: Sanskrit distinguishes between aspirated and unaspirated consonants (Ka vs. Kha, Ga vs. Gha, etc.) — a distinction that requires precise control of airflow and glottal tension. This aspiration contrast exercises the muscles of the larynx and the diaphragm, promoting respiratory health and vocal strength.

5. The Anusvāra and Visarga: The Anusvāra (Ṃ) — the nasal resonance that concludes every bījākṣara — creates a prolonged vibration in the nasal and cranial cavities that has documented effects on calming the nervous system and stimulating the sinuses and the pineal region. The Visarga (Ḥ) — the brief aspiration that follows certain vowels — creates a gentle release of breath that promotes relaxation and the release of held tension.

Phoneme-Body Correspondences

The traditional Indian understanding maps specific Sanskrit phonemes to specific parts of the body:

413
From the Eternal to the Expressed
Phoneme Category Articulation Point Body Correspondence Therapeutic Effect
Gutturals (Ka-varga) Throat (kaṇṭha) Thyroid, parathyroid, throat Thyroid regulation, voice strength
Palatals (Ca-varga) Palate (tālu) Pituitary, upper brain Hormonal balance, clarity
Retroflexes (Ṭa-varga) Roof of mouth (mūrdha) Brain, cranium Mental clarity, headache relief
Dentals (Ta-varga) Teeth (danta) Lungs, chest Respiratory health, chest opening
Labials (Pa-varga) Lips (oṣṭha) Heart, circulation Cardiac health, emotional balance
Semi-vowels (Ya-Ra-La-Va) Various Joints, ligaments Flexibility, movement
Sibilants (Śa-Ṣa-Sa) Various Nervous system Calming, nerve regeneration
Ha Glottis Diaphragm, prāṇa Breath deepening, energy

When these phonemes appear in Dīkṣitar's and Śyāma Śāstri's compositions — as they inevitably do, since the compositions are in Sanskrit — they activate these body correspondences in the singer. The act of singing a Dīkṣitar kṛti is simultaneously an act of full-body phonemic therapy. Every Sanskrit syllable exercises a specific part of the vocal apparatus, stimulates a specific set of nerves, and resonates in a specific region of the body.

The Healing Power of Compound Sounds

Beyond individual phonemes, Sanskrit employs compound sounds (saṃyuktākṣaras) — combinations of consonants that create complex articulatory gestures. Words like "brahma," "kṣetra," "jñāna," "śrīṃ," and "dhyāna" require the vocal apparatus to execute rapid, precise sequences of movements that:

  1. Exercise the articulatory muscles (tongue, lips, jaw, soft palate) in ways that simple sounds do not

  2. Create complex vibratory patterns that affect the cranial and thoracic cavities

414
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

  1. Require sustained attention — the mind must be fully present to produce these sounds correctly, making Sanskrit chanting a natural form of mindfulness practice

Dīkṣitar's compositions are particularly rich in compound sounds. His characteristic opening phrases — often beginning with the deity's name in its full Sanskrit form, laden with compound consonants — function as sonic power-punches that immediately activate multiple body regions and command full attention.

Dīkṣitar's Phonemic Intentionality

Consider Dīkṣitar's kṛti "Śrī Subrahmaṇyāya Namaste" (Rāga Kāmbhoji, Melakarta 28 Janya):

The opening phrase "Śrī Subrahmaṇyāya" contains:

  • Ś (palatal sibilant) — activates the palate and upper brain

  • r (retroflex continuant) — activates the cranial region

  • ī (long front vowel) — creates sustained nasal-cranial resonance

  • S (dental sibilant) — activates the teeth and frontal sinuses

  • u (back rounded vowel) — opens the throat and chest

  • b (labial stop) — activates the lips and heart region

  • r (again) — cranial activation

  • a (open vowel) — opens the entire vocal tract

  • h (glottal aspirate) — activates the diaphragm and deepens the breath

  • m (labial nasal) — activates the sinuses and nasal cavity

  • a (again) — full vocal tract opening

  • ṇ (retroflex nasal) — powerful cranial-nasal vibration

  • y (palatal glide) — smooth palatal activation

  • ā (long open vowel) — sustained full-body resonance

  • y (again) — palatal

  • a (again) — open

In just one word — "Subrahmaṇyāya" — the singer has activated the palate, the cranium, the throat, the chest, the lips, the sinuses, the diaphragm, and the nasal

415
From the Eternal to the Expressed

cavity. This is not a coincidence. Dīkṣitar chose Sanskrit precisely because of its phonemic richness, and he chose his words not only for their devotional meaning but for their therapeutic sound-profile.

Chapter 1.5: The Trinity of Carnatic Composition: Dīkṣitar, Śyāma Śāstri, and the Vedāntic Substratum

Pages 27–32

The Musical Trinity (Saṅgīta Trimūrti)

The period from approximately 1750 to 1850 CE witnessed the flowering of Carnatic music's greatest composers, three of whom — all born in the temple town of Tiruvārūr in the Tanjore district of Tamil Nadu — came to be known as the "Trinity" (Trimūrti) of Carnatic music:

  1. Tyāgarāja (1767–1847): The most prolific, composing primarily in Telugu, devoted to Rāma, emphasizing bhakti (devotion) and the emotional power of music.

  2. Muttuswāmi Dīkṣitar (1775–1835): The most erudite, composing primarily in Sanskrit, incorporating mantra, yantra, and Śrī Vidyā elements, emphasizing the cosmic and esoteric dimensions of music.

  3. Śyāma Śāstri (1762–1827): The most emotionally intense, composing primarily in Telugu with significant Sanskrit, devoted to the Goddess Kāmākṣī, emphasizing the transformative power of emotional surrender.

For the purposes of this work, we focus on Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri, whose Sanskrit-rich compositions and whose deep engagement with goddess worship and Vedāntic philosophy make them the most relevant to our investigation of the healing dimensions of the 72 Melakartas and 22 Śrutis.

Muttuswāmi Dīkṣitar: The Mantra-Maker

Dīkṣitar was not merely a composer; he was a mantravādin — a wielder of sacred formulae. His compositions are structured as mantras, with each element — the rāga choice, the tāla choice, the Sanskrit text, the melodic movement, even the specific placement of specific syllables on

416
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

specific notes — serving a ritual and therapeutic purpose.

Key features of Dīkṣitar's compositional approach:

1. Rāga Mudra (Rāga Signature): Dīkṣitar invariably embeds the name of the rāga within the Sanskrit text of the composition. This is not merely a signature device; it is a mantric identification — a declaration that the words and the melody are one, that the meaning and the sound are inseparable, that the healing power of the rāga is activated by naming it within the devotional context.

Example: In "Bālasubrahmanyam" (Rāga Surāṭi), the word "surāṭi" or a derivation appears in the sāhitya, fusing the rāga's identity with the devotional text.

2. Yantra Encoding: Several of Dīkṣitar's composition cycles — notably the Kāmalāmbā Navāvaraṇa Kṛtis — encode the structure of Śrī Cakra (the sacred geometric diagram of Śrī Vidyā) within their musical and textual architecture. Each kṛti corresponds to one of the nine āvaraṇas (enclosures) of the Śrī Cakra, and the rāga, tāla, and sāhitya of each kṛti are chosen to resonate with the specific deities, mantras, and energies of that āvaraṇa.

3. Navagraha Kṛtis: Dīkṣitar composed a set of nine kṛtis, one for each of the Navagrahas (nine planets), each in a rāga traditionally associated with that planet. These compositions are used therapeutically — specific kṛtis are prescribed for specific planetary afflictions, functioning as astrological-musical remedies.

4. Pañcabhūta and Pañcaliṅga Kṛtis: These cycles address the five elements (bhūtas) and the five sacred Śiva liṅgas of South India, respectively. Each kṛti's rāga is chosen to resonate with the specific element or sacred site, creating a sonic pilgrimage that the singer and listener can undertake without leaving their meditation seat.

Śyāma Śāstri: The Heart-Opener

If Dīkṣitar is the architect of sonic temples, Śyāma Śāstri is the breaker of emotional dams. His compositions — fewer in number (around 300, compared to Dīkṣitar's 400+) but extraordinary in emotional depth — specialize in the transformation of emotional suffering into devotional ecstasy.

Key features of Śyāma Śāstri's compositional approach:

1. Emotional Intensity: Śyāma Śāstri's compositions are characterized by a raw, unguarded emotionality that is rare in Carnatic music. His addresses to the Goddess Kāmākṣī often take the form of complaints, pleas, reproaches, and desperate appeals

417
From the Eternal to the Expressed

— "Why do you not look at me? Why do you ignore my suffering? Are you not the Mother of all?" This emotional directness creates a cathartic experience for the singer and listener, allowing buried emotions to surface and be released in the safe container of devotion.

2. Rhythmic Complexity: Śyāma Śāstri was the supreme master of the svarājati and the varṇam — two compositional forms that demand extraordinary rhythmic precision and stamina. The sheer physical effort of performing these compositions — the precise placement of syllables within complex rhythmic cycles, the sustained attention required, the coordination of breath, voice, and meaning — constitutes a form of musical tapas (austerity) that transforms the performer at every level.

3. The Goddess as Healer: In Śyāma Śāstri's theology, the Goddess Kāmākṣī is not a distant, abstract deity. She is Amma — Mother — the intimate, present, caring healer who responds to the devotee's suffering with grace. His compositions create a therapeutic relationship between the singer and the Divine Feminine, in which the singer's pain is offered up and the Goddess's healing is received.

The Vedāntic Substratum

Both Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri, despite their different temperaments and approaches, share a common philosophical foundation: Advaita Vedānta — the non-dual philosophy systematized by Śaṅkarācārya.

Advaita Vedānta teaches that:

  1. Brahman (the infinite, formless, blissful Absolute) is the only reality.

  2. The world (including the individual body-mind) is Māyā — an appearance that is neither fully real nor fully unreal.

  3. The individual self (Ātman) is identical with Brahman. The apparent separation between self and Absolute is an illusion caused by ignorance (avidyā).

  4. Liberation (mokṣa) consists in the direct recognition of this identity — "Aham Brahmāsmi" ("I am Brahman").

This philosophy pervades both Dīkṣitar's and Śyāma Śāstri's compositions:

418
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

  • Dīkṣitar embeds Vedāntic mahāvākyas (great sentences) within his sāhityas. In his composition on Goddess Kāmalāmbā, he declares: "cidānanda rūpiṇīm" — "She whose form is consciousness-bliss" — identifying the personal Goddess with the impersonal Brahman of Vedānta.

  • Śyāma Śāstri enacts the Vedāntic journey in the emotional trajectory of his compositions. The movement from suffering (duḥkha) to surrender (prapatti) to grace (anugraha) to bliss (ānanda) that characterizes his kṛtis is the emotional equivalent of the Vedāntic movement from ignorance to knowledge to liberation.

The Healing Implications

The Vedāntic substratum is itself the deepest level of healing:

  • At the physical level, the body's diseases are addressed by the rāga's vibrational properties.

  • At the emotional level, the mind's afflictions are addressed by the rāga's aesthetic personality and the sāhitya's devotional content.

  • At the existential level, the soul's fundamental ignorance is addressed by the Vedāntic truth embedded in the sāhitya — the truth that the suffering self and the healing Self are one.

This three-level healing is precisely what distinguishes the compositions of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri from mere entertainment or even mere devotional expression. They are complete therapeutic interventions — addressing body, mind, and soul simultaneously through the integrated medium of Śruti, Rāga, and Sanskrit Sāhitya.

Chapter 1.6: Śaṅkarācārya's Metaphorical Literature: Bhaja Govindam to Saundaryalaharī

Pages 33–38

Śaṅkarācārya: The Philosopher-Poet

Ādi Śaṅkarācārya (788–820 CE) is primarily known as the greatest exponent of Advaita Vedānta — the philosophy of non-duality. His philosophical commentaries (bhāṣyas) on the Upaniṣads, the Brahma Sūtras, and the Bhagavad Gītā are monuments of intellectual rigor. But Śaṅkara was also a poet of extraordinary power — a master of

419
From the Eternal to the Expressed

metaphor, simile, paradox, and devotional ecstasy whose compositions span the entire range from the austerely philosophical (Vivekacūḍāmaṇi) to the rapturously devotional (Saundaryalaharī).

For the purposes of this work, Śaṅkara's literary compositions are significant because they provide the philosophical and metaphorical framework within which the healing power of the 72 Melakartas and 22 Śrutis can be fully understood. The kṛtis of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri are the medicine; Śaṅkara's literature is the diagnosis — the clear-eyed, unsentimental, yet ultimately compassionate analysis of the human condition that reveals why we need healing and what true healing consists of.

Bhaja Govindam: The Diagnosis of Suffering

The Bhaja Govindam (also known as Moha Mudgara, "The Hammer Against Delusion") is perhaps Śaṅkara's most famous devotional poem. Its 31 verses are a relentless, compassionate, sometimes shocking exposition of the futility of worldly attachment and the urgency of spiritual realization.

"bhaja govindaṃ bhaja govindaṃ, govindaṃ bhaja mūḍha-mate | samprāpte sannihite kāle, nahi nahi rakṣati ḍukṛñ-karaṇe ||"

"Worship Govinda, worship Govinda, worship Govinda, O fool! When the appointed time (death) arrives, rules of grammar will not save you."

This opening verse is a masterpiece of therapeutic shock. It shatters the listener's complacency by confronting them with the reality of mortality. The repeated imperative "bhaja govindaṃ" (worship Govinda) is not merely a devotional injunction; it is a mantra — a rhythmically repeated, phonetically potent phrase that, when chanted, activates the heart center and redirects the mind toward the essential.

The verse's therapeutic mechanism operates on multiple levels:

Physical Level: The repeated "bha" (labial voiced stop) resonates in the chest; "ja" (palatal voiced stop) activates the palate; "go" (guttural + back vowel) opens the throat; "vin" (labio-dental + nasal) activates the sinuses; "daṃ" (dental + anusvāra) creates cranial resonance. The entire phrase is a circuit of full-body sonic activation.

Mental Level: The confrontation with mortality (the "diagnosis") creates a productive crisis in the listener's habitual mental patterns. Psychotherapists recognize this as the moment of "creative disorganization" — the breaking apart of dysfunctional patterns that is the prerequisite for healing reorganization.

420
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

Soul Level: The instruction to "worship Govinda" points beyond the crisis to the solution — the turn toward the divine, the recognition that the Self is not the mortal body or the anxious mind but the infinite consciousness (Govinda = "finder of cows" = "finder of the senses" = the Self who knows all experience from within).

Vivekacūḍāmaṇi: The Discrimination That Heals

The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi ("Crest-Jewel of Discrimination") is Śaṅkara's most comprehensive prakaraṇa grantha (independent philosophical treatise). In 580 verses, it guides the student from the initial recognition of suffering through the practice of discrimination (viveka) to the final realization of identity with Brahman.

The text's healing power lies in its sustained application of discernment — the methodical separation of the real (Ātman/Brahman) from the unreal (the body, the mind, the ego). Verse after verse, Śaṅkara peels away layers of false identification:

"na deho na prāṇo na ca sukhacid ātmā na ca mano, na buddhir nāhaṅkṛtir iti neti prakriyayā | nivṛtte sarvopalabdhi-karāṇe śeṣa-bhūtaḥ svayaṃ-jyotiḥ ātmā paramārtha-satyaḥ ||"

"Not the body, not the prāṇa, not the mind, not the intellect, not the ego — by the process of 'not this, not this,' when all objects of experience have been negated, what remains is the Self-luminous Self — the ultimate truth."

This "neti neti" (not this, not this) process is the ultimate diagnostic procedure — the identification and rejection of everything that is NOT the source of health, NOT the source of wholeness, NOT the Self. When all that is not-Self has been stripped away, what remains is pure, limitless, blissful consciousness — and this consciousness is the ultimate healing agent.

The metaphor of the "crest-jewel" (cūḍāmaṇi) is itself therapeutic: discrimination is not a heavy, burdensome, ascetic practice but a jewel — beautiful, precious, light, and adorning. The one who discriminates between the real and the unreal is crowned, not diminished; enriched, not impoverished.

Ātmabodha: The Self-Knowledge That Cures

The Ātmabodha ("Self-Knowledge") is a brief (68 verses) but extraordinarily potent text that distills the essence of Advaita Vedānta into accessible, metaphor-rich verses.

421
From the Eternal to the Expressed

"āvirbhūtaṃ yathā meghair arka-maṇḍalaṃ nirmalam | tathā ajñāna-nivṛttyā ca svātmā prakāśate sphuṭam ||"

"Just as the clear disc of the sun appears when the clouds disperse, so the pure Self shines forth clearly when ignorance is removed."

This solar metaphor is healing at every level:

Physical: The image of the sun activates the internal visualization of warmth and light, which has documented effects on mood, circadian rhythm, and vitamin D metabolism. Even the mental image of sunlight can shift neurochemistry toward serotonin production.

Mental: The metaphor reframes the problem of suffering. Suffering is not caused by the presence of something bad; it is caused by the absence of something good — or rather, by the obscuration of something that is always present. The Self is always shining; only the clouds of ignorance hide it. This reframing is profoundly therapeutic because it means that healing does not require the creation of something new but the removal of something false.

Soul: The identification of the Self with the sun — self-luminous, all-illuminating, always present — is the direct transmission of Advaitic truth. To truly understand this verse is to be healed at the deepest level, because the understanding itself IS the healing. Knowledge of the Self is not a preliminary to liberation; it IS liberation.

Saundaryalaharī: The Wave of Beauty

The Saundaryalaharī ("Wave of Beauty") is Śaṅkara's supreme devotional masterpiece — 100 verses describing the beauty, power, and grace of the Goddess (Devī/Śakti/Tripurasundarī). The first 41 verses (the Ānandalaharī, "Wave of Bliss") are traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara's direct experience and deal with the Tantric/Śrī Vidyā dimensions of goddess worship. The remaining 59 verses (the Saundaryalaharī proper) describe the Goddess's physical beauty from head to toe, using an extraordinary profusion of metaphor.

This text is relevant to our study for several reasons:

1. Mantra Encoding: Each verse of the Saundaryalaharī is associated with a specific yantra (geometric diagram), a specific mantra, and a specific therapeutic application. The traditional commentary literature prescribes specific verses for specific ailments — verse X for eye diseases, verse Y for fertility, verse Z for protection from enemies, etc.

422
THE ŚRUTI-RĀGA-SANSKRIT HEALING MATRIX

This is Rāga Cikitsā's literary equivalent — poetry as prescription.

2. The Goddess-Body as Sound-Body: The detailed description of the Goddess's body in verses 42–100 is simultaneously a description of the Mātṛkā (the Sanskrit alphabet as the Goddess's body) and, by extension, of the entire system of sacred sound. When Śaṅkara describes the Goddess's eyes, he is describing the vowels A and Ā; when he describes her throat, he is describing the Viśuddha chakra and its 16 vowel-petals; when he describes her navel, he is describing the Maṇipūra and its 10 consonant-petals.

3. Beauty as Healing: The Saundaryalaharī's central premise is that beauty heals. The contemplation of the Goddess's beauty — through the medium of Sanskrit poetry — transforms the devotee's consciousness, dissolving the barriers of ego, fear, and ignorance that obstruct the natural flow of health. This is not a superficial aestheticism; it is a recognition that beauty (saundarya) is a fundamental quality of Brahman itself, and that contact with beauty in any form — visual, auditory, linguistic — is contact with the healing ground of being.

4. Connection to Dīkṣitar: Dīkṣitar's Kāmalāmbā Navāvaraṇa Kṛtis are directly modeled on the Saundaryalaharī's Śrī Vidyā framework. The rāga choices, the sāhitya structure, and the mantra encoding of these kṛtis reflect a deep engagement with Śaṅkara's text. To study the Saundaryalaharī is to understand the philosophical and ritual background of Dīkṣitar's most ambitious compositional project.

Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotram: Silence as the Supreme Teaching

The Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotram describes Śiva as the silent teacher — the young guru who sits facing south (dakṣiṇa) and teaches the four aged sages through silence (mauna). This text provides the ultimate philosophical frame for understanding the healing power of sound:

"citram vaṭa-taror mūle vṛddhāḥ śiṣyā gururyuvā | gurostu maunaṃ vyākhyānaṃ śiṣyāstu chinna-saṃśayāḥ ||"

"Wonderful! Beneath the banyan tree, the students are old, the teacher is young. The teacher's exposition is silence, and the students' doubts are resolved."

The supreme teaching is silence — and silence is the ground from which all sound arises and to which all sound returns. The 22 Śrutis emerge from silence and dissolve into silence. The 72 Melakartas are organized patterns of sound floating in an ocean of

423
From the Eternal to the Expressed

silence. The Sanskrit sāhitya of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri begins in silence, moves through sound, and culminates in silence.

The ultimate healing is the recognition that the Self is this silence — the awareness that precedes, underlies, and survives all sound. Sound heals the body and the mind; silence heals the soul. And the greatest music — the greatest compositions of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri, performed with full awareness of the 22 Śrutis and the 72 Melakartas — takes the listener on exactly this journey: from suffering, through sound, to silence, to the Self.

Chapter 1.7: The Concept of Rāga Cikitsā: Music as Medicine

Pages 39–43

Historical Foundations

The use of music as medicine — Rāga Cikitsā (rāga + cikitsā, "treatment") — is attested in Indian literature from the earliest periods.

The Sāma Veda itself is, in a sense, a therapeutic text — its melodies were designed not merely to please the gods but to harmonize the cosmic order and, by extension, the human organism that participates in that order.

Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra (2nd century BCE – 2nd century CE), while primarily a treatise on dramaturgy, contains extensive discussions of rasa (aesthetic emotion) and its effects on the audience — effects that are described in terms remarkably similar to those used in Āyurvedic medicine to describe the effects of drugs and therapies.

Śārṅgadeva's Saṅgīta Ratnākara (13th century) explicitly discusses the therapeutic properties of rāgas and their ability to cure specific diseases.

The Rāga Cikitsā tradition, as practiced in various parts of India (particularly in the courts of the Tanjore and Mysore kingdoms), maintained a systematic body of knowledge about which rāgas are appropriate for which conditions:

The Mechanism of Rāga Healing

How does a rāga heal? Several mechanisms operate simultaneously:

1. Frequency Resonance: Each Śruti has a specific frequency. When this frequency is sustained through vocal or instrumental performance, it creates sympathetic vibrations in the listener's body — in specific organs, tissues, and energy centers. The principle is identical to the phenomenon of acoustic resonance: when a tuning fork is struck near a piano, the piano string tuned to the same frequency will begin to vibrate spontaneously.

The human body contains multiple resonant cavities — the skull, the chest, the abdomen, the sinuses — each with its own natural resonant frequency. When a rāga employs Śrutis that match these frequencies, the corresponding body cavities resonate, promoting blood flow, nerve activation, and energy movement in those regions.

425
From the Eternal to the Expressed

2. Entrainment: The rhythmic and melodic patterns of a rāga tend to entrain — synchronize — the listener's biological rhythms (heartbeat, breathing rate, brainwave frequency). A slow, meditative rāga like Nīlāmbari will slow the heartbeat and deepen the breathing; a vigorous, energetic rāga like Bihāg will quicken them. This entrainment is involuntary and operates even when the listener is not consciously attending to the music.

3. Emotional Catharsis: Each rāga has a characteristic rasa — a dominant emotional quality. When the listener is exposed to a rāga whose rasa corresponds to a blocked or suppressed emotion, the music provides a safe, structured container for that emotion to emerge, be experienced, and be released. This is the mechanism behind the therapeutic use of "sad" rāgas for grief — the music does not increase sadness; it releases it, allowing the listener to move through the emotion rather than remaining stuck in it.

4. Cognitive Restructuring: The Sanskrit sāhitya (text) of a kṛti conveys specific ideas — about the nature of the divine, the nature of the self, the impermanence of suffering, the availability of grace. When these ideas are carried by the emotional power of the rāga and the vibrational precision of the Śruti, they bypass the listener's cognitive defenses and enter the deeper layers of the mind, where they can effect lasting changes in belief, attitude, and self-understanding.

5. Spiritual Transmission: In the Indian understanding, a rāga performed with full devotion and Śruti-precision becomes a vehicle for divine grace (anugraha). The Goddess — or Śiva, or Viṣṇu, or whichever deity is invoked in the sāhitya — is understood to be literally present in the sound, and the listener's exposure to that sound is an act of darśana (sacred seeing/hearing) that transforms at the deepest level.

Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri as Healers

Both Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri composed with healing intent:

Dīkṣitar's Navagraha Kṛtis are explicitly therapeutic — they are prescribed for specific planetary afflictions that, according to Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology), cause specific physical and psychological diseases.

Śyāma Śāstri's emotional compositions are therapeutic through their capacity to open the heart — to dissolve the emotional armoring that blocks the flow of prāṇa and creates conditions for physical disease.

Both composers were steeped in the tradition of Rāga Cikitsā, and their compositions represent the highest flowering of this tradition — the point at which music, mantra, philosophy, and therapy converge in a single, integrated practice.

Chapter 1.8: Nāda Yoga: The Inner Physician of Sound

The Practice of Inner Listening

Nāda Yoga — the yoga of sound — is the contemplative discipline that forms the experiential foundation for all that we have discussed. Without the practice of deep listening, the theoretical knowledge of Śrutis, Melakartas, and Sanskrit phonetics remains intellectual and abstract. With the practice, it becomes alive, immediate, and healing.

The Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā (Chapter IV) describes the practice:

"The yogī, seated in Muktāsana, with mind collected through Śāmbhavī Mudrā, should listen to the sound within the right ear."

The practitioner closes the ears (using Yoni Mudrā or Ṣaṇmukhī Mudrā) and listens to the subtle sounds that arise within. These sounds — initially heard as buzzing, humming, tinkling, or ringing — become progressively more refined and more musical as the practice deepens:

  1. Stage One: Physical sounds (heartbeat, blood flow, nerve activity)

  2. Stage Two: Subtle sounds (bells, flutes, drums — the ten stages of Anāhata Nāda)

  3. Stage Three: Causal sound (a single, pure, sustained tone — the Praṇava OṂ)

  4. Stage Four: Transcendent silence (the sound dissolves into the soundless awareness that is Brahman)

This practice is the inner laboratory in which the 22 Śrutis are directly perceived, the 72 Melakartas are directly experienced (as patterns within the inner sound), and the healing power of Sanskrit is directly verified.

427
From the Eternal to the Expressed

Nāda Yoga and the Brain

Modern neuroscience is beginning to understand the mechanisms underlying Nāda Yoga:

  1. Tinnitus and the auditory cortex: The inner sounds of Nāda Yoga are related to the spontaneous activity of the auditory cortex. In tinnitus (pathological inner sound), this activity is perceived as disturbing; in Nāda Yoga, the same activity is perceived as meaningful and is used as a meditation object. The difference lies in the relationship of consciousness to the sound — aversion vs. equanimity.

  2. Default mode network: Nāda Yoga practice quiets the default mode network (DMN) — the brain network associated with self-referential thinking, rumination, and the ego. As the DMN quiets, the practitioner experiences a dissolution of the ordinary sense of self and an expansion into a more spacious, peaceful awareness.

  3. Gamma wave activity: Advanced Nāda Yoga practitioners show increased gamma wave activity — high-frequency brainwaves associated with heightened awareness, insight, and the integration of information from multiple brain regions.

  4. Vagal tone: The closed-ear, inward-listening posture of Nāda Yoga stimulates the vagus nerve (via the auricular branch), increasing vagal tone and promoting parasympathetic dominance — a state associated with healing, regeneration, and emotional equilibrium.

The Five Kośas and Music

The Taittirīya Upaniṣad describes five kośas (sheaths) of the human being:

  1. Annamaya Kośa (food/physical sheath) → healed by Śruti (precise frequency)

  2. Prāṇamaya Kośa (breath/energy sheath) → healed by Tāla (rhythm, which entrains breathing)

  3. Manomaya Kośa (mind/emotional sheath) → healed by Rāga (melody, which shapes emotion)

  4. Vijñānamaya Kośa (wisdom/intellectual sheath) → healed by Sāhitya (Sanskrit meaning)

  5. Ānandamaya Kośa (bliss sheath) → healed by Bhakti (devotion, which dissolves the ego)

A complete kṛti by Dīkṣitar or Śyāma Śāstri — performed with correct Śruti, appropriate Tāla, the specific Rāga, the Sanskrit Sāhitya, and genuine Bhakti — addresses all five kośas simultaneously. It is, literally, complete medicine — a therapeutic intervention that reaches every layer of the human being.

Chapter 2.1: The Vedic Origins of the 22 Śrutis: Nāradīya Śikṣā and Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra

Pages 51–56

The Antiquity of the 22-Śruti System

The identification of 22 microtonal intervals within the octave is one of the most ancient and most distinctive contributions of Indian civilization to the science of sound. While other musical cultures have recognized the existence of microtones — Arab maqām theory identifies quarter-tones, and Chinese music employs subtle pitch inflections — none has developed a system as mathematically precise, as philosophically grounded, or as therapeutically elaborated as the Indian 22-Śruti system.

The earliest textual references to the 22 Śrutis appear in:

1. Nāradīya Śikṣā (attributed to the sage Nārada, date uncertain but possibly as early as the 1st century BCE): This text, primarily concerned with the correct pronunciation of Vedic mantras, contains sections on musical theory that describe the seven svaras and their Śruti intervals. The Nāradīya Śikṣā establishes the fundamental principle that each svara "occupies" a specific number of Śrutis, and that the total number within the octave is 22.

2. Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra (2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE): This encyclopedic treatise on the performing arts contains the most detailed early treatment of the 22 Śrutis. Bharata describes:

  • The names of the 22 Śrutis

  • Their distribution among the seven svaras (4-3-2-4-4-3-2)

431
From the Eternal to the Expressed

  • The experimental method by which they can be demonstrated (the two-vīṇā experiment)

  • Their aesthetic and emotional properties

3. Dattilam (approximately contemporary with the Nāṭyaśāstra): This brief but important text provides additional detail on the Śruti system and its relationship to jāti (melodic types) and rāga.

Bharata's Two-Vīṇā Experiment

Bharata describes a remarkable experimental procedure for demonstrating the 22 Śrutis:

"Two vīṇās should be tuned in perfect unison. Then, on the first vīṇā, let Sa remain unchanged. On the second vīṇā, lower the pitch of Sa by one Śruti. The resulting interval — the smallest perceptible difference in pitch — is one Śruti."

By systematically lowering the pitch of successive strings on the second vīṇā by one Śruti at a time, and noting the points at which the intervals coincide with the natural positions of the seven svaras, Bharata demonstrates that exactly 22 Śruti-steps are required to traverse the octave.

This experiment is significant for several reasons:

  1. It is empirical. It relies on direct auditory perception, not on mathematical calculation or philosophical speculation.

  2. It establishes the Śruti as a perceptual unit. A Śruti is not an abstract mathematical ratio; it is the smallest interval that a trained musician can reliably hear. This grounds the entire system in human perception — in the actual capabilities of the human ear and brain.

  3. It is reproducible. Any musician with two properly made vīṇās can replicate the experiment and verify the results.

The Nāradīya Śikṣā's Vedic Connection

The Nāradīya Śikṣā places the Śruti system within a specifically Vedic context. It describes the seven svaras as arising from the sounds of animals and natural phenomena:

432
THE MICROTONAL ANATOMY OF HEALING SOUND
Svara Animal/Natural Sound Quality
Sa (Ṣaḍja) Peacock Royal, announcing
Re (Ṛṣabha) Bull Powerful, grounding
Ga (Gāndhāra) Goat Plaintive, emotional
Ma (Madhyama) Crane Balanced, central
Pa (Pañcama) Cuckoo Sweet, harmonious
Dha (Dhaivata) Horse Energetic, noble
Ni (Niṣāda) Elephant Deep, majestic

These natural correspondences are not merely fanciful. They encode a deep understanding of the timbral and emotional quality of each svara. The peacock's cry has the announcing, regal quality of Sa (the tonic); the bull's bellow has the powerful, grounding quality of Re (the second); the goat's bleat has the plaintive, emotionally vulnerable quality of Ga (the third); and so on.

By grounding the svaras in natural sounds, the Nāradīya Śikṣā establishes the principle that music is not an artificial human construction but a participation in the natural sonic order of the world — an expression of Ṛta, the cosmic pattern. This principle has profound therapeutic implications: healing through music is not an imposition of human will upon the body but an alignment of the body with the natural order that it already participates in.

The 22 Śrutis and Vedic Chanting

The Vedic connection is deepened by the observation that the three Vedic accents — Udātta (raised), Anudātta (lowered), and Svarita (combined) — correspond to specific Śruti intervals:

  • The Udātta (high tone) is approximately one Śruti above the middle tone

  • The Anudātta (low tone) is approximately one Śruti below the middle tone

  • The Svarita (combined tone) involves a gliding movement across multiple Śrutis

This means that Vedic chanting is inherently microtonal — it employs Śruti-level pitch distinctions that are more subtle than those of ordinary speech. The therapeutic

433
From the Eternal to the Expressed

power of Vedic chanting lies, in part, in this microtonal precision: the subtle pitch inflections of Vedic recitation activate neural pathways that ordinary speech does not reach.

Dīkṣitar, who was deeply learned in Vedic chanting (his family held the hereditary position of temple musicians at Tiruvārūr), incorporated this Vedic microtonal sensibility into his Carnatic compositions. The characteristic "gamaka" (oscillation) in Dīkṣitar's style — the subtle, continuous variation of pitch around each note — reflects the Vedic understanding that a svara is not a fixed point but a living, breathing, oscillating reality defined by its Śruti range.

Chapter 2.2: The Distribution of 22 Śrutis Among the Saptasvaras

The 4-3-2-4-4-3-2 Pattern

The distribution of Śrutis among the seven svaras is not equal. Some svaras "contain" more Śrutis than others:

Sa: ████ (4 Śrutis) Re: ███ (3 Śrutis) Ga: ██ (2 Śrutis) Ma: ████ (4 Śrutis) Pa: ████ (4 Śrutis) Dha: ███ (3 Śrutis) Ni: ██ (2 Śrutis) Total: 22

This asymmetric distribution is one of the most profound features of the Indian tonal system. It means that the octave is not divided into equal parts (as in the Western 12-tone equal temperament system) but into unequal, qualitatively distinct regions, each with its own character, its own emotional weight, and its own healing property.

The Symmetry of the Distribution

Despite its asymmetry, the distribution reveals a beautiful higher-order symmetry:

Lower Tetrachord (Sa-Re-Ga-Ma): 4-3-2-4 = 13 Śrutis Upper Tetrachord (Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa): 4-3-2-(4) = 13 Śrutis (including the 4 Śrutis of the upper Sa)

The two tetrachords are mirror images of each other: the pattern 4-3-2 appears in both, reflecting the fundamental principle of saṃvāda (concordance) between the lower and upper halves of the scale.

This mirror symmetry has deep healing implications:

434
THE MICROTONAL ANATOMY OF HEALING SOUND

  1. Left-right brain balance: The lower tetrachord (Sa-Re-Ga-Ma), associated with stability and groundedness, tends to activate the left hemisphere (analytical, structured). The upper tetrachord (Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa), associated with expression and aspiration, tends to activate the right hemisphere (intuitive, creative). The mirror symmetry ensures that a rāga employing the full octave will balance both hemispheres.

  2. Anabolism-catabolism balance: The lower tetrachord corresponds to building up (anabolism) — the foundation of the scale, the establishment of tonal identity. The upper tetrachord corresponds to reaching out (catabolism) — the extension of the scale beyond its center, the aspiration toward the upper Sa. A complete rāga balances these metabolic tendencies.

  3. Earth-sky balance: The lower tetrachord is traditionally associated with the earth (pṛthivī), the upper with the sky (ākāśa). The mirror symmetry ensures that the musical experience is grounded in the earth while reaching toward the sky — embodied while aspiring to transcendence.

The Four Śrutis of Sa

The tonic (Sa) is assigned 4 Śrutis. This might seem paradoxical — isn't Sa a single, fixed pitch? — but it reflects a profound understanding:

  1. Sa is not absolutely fixed. The precise pitch of Sa varies from performer to performer, from instrument to instrument, from context to context. The 4 Śrutis of Sa represent the range of acceptable variation — the "bandwidth" within which Sa can be intoned while still functioning as a stable tonic.

  2. The 4 Śrutis encode the four stages of sound. Just as Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī represent four levels of sonic manifestation, the 4 Śrutis of Sa represent four levels of tonic presence — from the subtlest, most internalized hearing of Sa (Tīvrā = "intense," the inner awareness of the tonic) to the most externalized, most fully sounded Sa (Chandovatī = "rhythmic," the fully manifest tonic that establishes the metrical framework of the performance).

436
THE MICROTONAL ANATOMY OF HEALING SOUND

  1. The 4 Śrutis correspond to the 4 puruṣārthas. Dharma (righteousness), Artha (prosperity), Kāma (desire), and Mokṣa (liberation) — the four goals of human life — are encoded in the four Śrutis of the tonic. The tonic is the microcosm of the entire human enterprise; its four Śrutis represent the full range of human aspiration.

The Two Śrutis of Ga and Ni

Ga and Ni have only 2 Śrutis each, making them the most emotionally sensitive svaras. With less tonal "space" to move in, every slight change in the intonation of Ga or Ni produces a dramatic change in emotional quality. This is why:

  • Ga is the svara that most powerfully distinguishes major from minor (in Western terms). The two Śrutis of Ga correspond roughly to the major third (Krodhā, Śruti 9) and the minor third (Raudrī, Śruti 8). The difference between these two positions — a single Śruti — is the difference between joy and sorrow, between brightness and shadow.

  • Ni is the svara that most powerfully determines the "flavor" of the upper tetrachord. The two Śrutis of Ni correspond roughly to the major seventh (Kṣobhiṇī, Śruti 22) and the minor seventh (Ugrā, Śruti 21). The major seventh creates tension, aspiration, yearning for resolution; the minor seventh creates depth, mystery, introspection.

In Dīkṣitar's compositions, the treatment of Ga and Ni is often the signature of the rāga's therapeutic intention. In rāgas with Antara Gāndhāra (G3, the high Ga), the healing quality tends toward brightness, confidence, and energizing. In rāgas with Sādhāraṇa Gāndhāra (G2, the middle Ga), the quality tends toward warmth, empathy, and emotional connection. In rāgas with Śuddha Gāndhāra (G1, the low Ga), the quality tends toward introversion, contemplation, and deep stillness.

Chapter 2.3: Mathematical Ratios and Frequency Relationships

The Mathematics of Consonance

The 22 Śrutis are not arbitrarily placed along the octave. They are determined by specific mathematical ratios — relationships between frequencies that the human ear perceives as consonant, dissonant, or neutral.

The fundamental consonances are:

Interval Ratio Śruti Position Quality
Unison 1:1 Sa (Śruti 1) Perfect identity
Octave 2:1 Upper Sa Perfect completion
Perfect Fifth 3:2 Pa (Śruti 14) Perfect harmony
Perfect Fourth 4:3 Ma (Śruti 10) Perfect grounding
Major Third 5:4 Ga (Śruti 9) Sweet brightness
Minor Third 6:5 Ga (Śruti 8) Gentle pathos
Major Sixth 5:3 Dha (Śruti 20) Warm beauty
Minor Sixth 8:5 Dha (Śruti 19) Deep emotion
Major Second 9:8 or 10:9 Re (Śruti 7 or 6) Forward movement
Minor Second 16:15 Re (Śruti 5) Tension, yearning
Major Seventh 15:8 Ni (Śruti 22) Aspiration
Minor Seventh 16:9 Ni (Śruti 21) Depth

The Two Generating Principles

The 22 Śrutis can be generated by two complementary mathematical processes:

1. The Cycle of Fifths: Starting from Sa, ascending by perfect fifths (ratio 3:2) and bringing each resulting note back within the octave (by halving its frequency as many times as necessary), generates a series of tones. After 12 such steps, you arrive close to the starting Sa — but not exactly. The difference (the "Pythagorean comma") is

THE MICROTONAL ANATOMY OF HEALING SOUND

approximately 23.46 cents. This process generates the Pythagorean or cyclical version of the Śrutis.

2. The Harmonic Series: The natural overtones of any vibrating body — the 2nd harmonic (octave), 3rd (fifth), 4th (double octave), 5th (major third two octaves up), 6th (fifth an octave up), 7th (minor seventh), etc. — provide a different set of ratios. These are the just intonation or harmonic Śrutis, characterized by the pure, beatless quality of their intervals.

The Indian 22-Śruti system incorporates both generating principles. Some Śrutis are best understood as products of the cycle of fifths (particularly the Śrutis of Sa, Ma, and Pa); others are best understood as products of the harmonic series (particularly the Śrutis of Ga, Dha, and Ni). The system as a whole represents a synthesis of cyclical and harmonic thinking — a mathematical map of all the important frequency relationships that the human ear can perceive.

Healing Implications of Mathematical Ratios

The mathematical ratios of the Śrutis are not merely abstract numbers. They are prescriptions for specific vibratory experiences:

  • Simple ratios (1:1, 2:1, 3:2, 4:3) produce consonant intervals that the nervous system experiences as restful, harmonious, and integrating. These ratios are associated with the sattvic (pure, balanced) quality and are therapeutic for conditions involving agitation, fragmentation, and disharmony — anxiety, ADHD, insomnia, hypertension.

  • Moderately complex ratios (5:4, 6:5, 5:3, 8:5) produce sweet intervals that the nervous system experiences as emotionally moving, beautiful, and satisfying. These ratios are associated with the rajasic (active, passionate) quality in its positive form and are therapeutic for conditions involving emotional blockage, depression, and lack of motivation.

  • Highly complex ratios (9:8, 10:9, 16:15, 15:8, 16:9) produce tense intervals that the nervous system experiences as stimulating, challenging, and energizing. These ratios are associated with the rajasic quality in its more intense form and are therapeutic for conditions involving lethargy, stagnation, and kapha accumulation.

The 72 Melakarta system organizes these ratios into 72 distinct therapeutic profiles, each with its own balance of consonance, sweetness, and tension. This is the subject of Section III.

Chapter 2.4: The Two Śruti Traditions: Cyclical and Harmonic

Pages 69–73

The Pythagorean (Cyclical) Approach

In this approach, all intervals are derived from the cycle of perfect fifths (3:2 ratio). Starting from Sa:

scss

Copy code

Sa → Pa (3:2) → Re (9:8) → Dha (27:16) → Ga (81:64) → Ni (243:128) → Ma# (729:512)...

Each step multiplies the previous frequency by 3/2, then divides by 2 if necessary to stay within the octave. This generates a set of intervals with the following properties:

  • All fifths are pure (exactly 3:2)

  • All fourths are pure (exactly 4:3)

  • Thirds are slightly wide (81:64 instead of 5:4 for the major third)

  • The system is internally consistent but slightly "sharp" relative to natural harmonics

Healing quality of Pythagorean intervals: These intervals are bright, clear, angular, and structuring. They appeal to the intellect and the sense of order. They are therapeutic for conditions involving mental confusion, lack of discipline, and structural disorganization.

Dīkṣitar's compositions in rāgas that emphasize the Sa-Pa axis (rāgas with prominent use of the perfect fifth) tend to have a Pythagorean quality — bright, architecturally precise, intellectually satisfying.

440
THE MICROTONAL ANATOMY OF HEALING SOUND

The Harmonic (Just Intonation) Approach

In this approach, intervals are derived from the natural harmonic series — the overtones that any vibrating body produces:

java

Run CodeCopy code

Fundamental (1:1 = Sa) 2nd harmonic (2:1 = Upper Sa) 3rd harmonic (3:2 = Pa) 4th harmonic (4:3 → Ma by inversion) 5th harmonic (5:4 = Ga "pure major third") 6th harmonic (6:5 → Ga "pure minor third" via different derivation) 7th harmonic (7:4 → Ni "natural seventh")

This generates intervals that are:

  • Beatless (perfectly consonant, with no audible interference patterns)

  • Warm and resonant

  • "Natural" in quality — the ear recognizes them immediately as consonant

Healing quality of harmonic intervals: These intervals are warm, resonant, enveloping, and emotionally moving. They appeal to the heart and the emotions. They are therapeutic for conditions involving emotional coldness, disconnection, alienation, and lack of empathy.

Śyāma Śāstri's compositions, with their characteristic emotional warmth and their emphasis on the expressive potential of Ga and Ni, tend to have a harmonic-just-intonation quality — warm, resonant, heart-opening.

The Indian Synthesis

The genius of the 22-Śruti system is that it includes both Pythagorean and harmonic intervals within a single framework. This allows the Indian musician to choose, moment by moment, between the bright clarity of Pythagorean intonation and the warm resonance of harmonic intonation — or to blend the two in various proportions.

This flexibility is one of the sources of Indian music's extraordinary therapeutic range. A rāga performed with primarily Pythagorean Śrutis will have a different healing quality than the same rāga performed with primarily harmonic Śrutis. The skilled performer — and the skilled Rāga Cikitsā practitioner — adjusts the Śruti values to match the therapeutic need of the listener.

Chapter 2.5: Śruti and Bhāva: How Microtones Create Emotional States

Pages 74–78

The Śruti-Bhāva Connection

Bhāva (भाव) — literally "being" or "becoming" — refers in musical and theatrical contexts to the specific emotional state evoked by a performance. The Nāṭyaśāstra identifies eight (later nine) primary bhāvas or rasas:

Rasa Meaning Dominant Śruti Region
Śṛṅgāra Love/Beauty Ga (8-9), Ni (21-22): sweet thirds and sevenths
Hāsya Humor/Joy Re (6-7), Dha (19-20): bright seconds and sixths
Karuṇa Compassion/Sorrow Ga (8), Ni (21): minor thirds and sevenths
Raudra Anger/Ferocity All sharp/tense intervals
Vīra Heroism/Courage Sa (1-4), Pa (14-17): strong tonic and fifth
Bhayānaka Fear/Terror Ga (8), Dha (18): diminished intervals
Bībhatsa Disgust/Aversion Dissonant combinations
Adbhuta Wonder/Amazement Unusual Śruti combinations
Śānta Peace/Tranquility Sa (1), Pa (14): pure consonances

The relationship between Śruti values and emotional states is not arbitrary. It is grounded in the psychoacoustic properties of intervals:

  • Consonant intervals (small-number ratios) are perceived as stable, restful, and peaceful → Śānta rasa

  • Moderately dissonant intervals (medium-number ratios) are perceived as emotionally moving, tender, and bittersweet → Śṛṅgāra and Karuṇa rasas

  • Strongly dissonant intervals (large-number ratios) are perceived as tense, energetic, and challenging → Raudra and Vīra rasas

How Dīkṣitar Uses Śruti for Bhāva

Dīkṣitar's genius lies in his ability to create precise emotional effects through precise

442
THE MICROTONAL ANATOMY OF HEALING SOUND

Śruti choices. Consider his kṛti "Mīnākṣī me mudam dehi" (Rāga Gamakakriyā, Melakarta 53):

Rāga Gamakakriyā uses: Sa, R1, G3, M2, Pa, D1, N3

The combination of R1 (low Re, Śruti 5 — Dayāvatī, "compassionate") with G3 (high Ga, Śruti 9 — Krodhā, "fierce") creates a wide interval between the second and third degrees — an interval that conveys yearning, stretching, aspiration. This perfectly matches the sāhitya's content: "Mīnākṣī, give me bliss" — the devotee stretching toward the Goddess, yearning for her grace.

The M2 (Prati Madhyama) adds a note of sharpness and urgency — the yearning is not passive but active, insistent, passionate.

The D1 (low Dha, Śruti 18 — Madantī, "intoxicating") combined with N3 (high Ni, Śruti 22 — Kṣobhiṇī, "agitating") creates a similar wide interval in the upper tetrachord, mirroring the lower tetrachord's yearning quality and establishing a whole-octave therapeutic field of aspiration and grace.

How Śyāma Śāstri Uses Śruti for Bhāva

Śyāma Śāstri's approach is different but equally precise. Consider his masterpiece "O Jagadambā" (Rāga Ānandabhairavī):

Rāga Ānandabhairavī (a janya of Melakarta 20, Naṭabhairavī) uses: Sa, R2, G2, Ma, Pa, D2, N2

This scale is rich in middle-position Śrutis — R2 (Śruti 6, Ranjanī, "pleasing"), G2 (Śruti 8, Raudrī, "fierce" — but in context, "poignant"), D2 (Śruti 19, Rohiṇī, "growing"), N2 (Śruti 21, Ugrā, "powerful"). The overall Śruti profile is one of moderate tension with emotional warmth — not the bright clarity of major-mode rāgas, not the deep darkness of highly dissonant rāgas, but a twilight quality — tender, vulnerable, infinitely human.

This Śruti profile perfectly supports the sāhitya: "O Mother of the universe!" — the cry of a child to its mother, simultaneously powerful and vulnerable, demanding and surrendering. The "moderate tension" of the intervals creates the space for emotional catharsis — the listener can feel the devotee's pain, participate in it, and then experience the release that comes when the Goddess responds.

Chapter 2.6: Śruti in Dīkṣitar's Compositions: Microtonal Mastery in Practice

Pages 79–83

Dīkṣitar's Microtonal Signature

Dīkṣitar's compositions are distinguished by an extraordinary attention to Śruti — an attention that reflects his training in Vedic chanting, his knowledge of mantra śāstra, and his deep understanding of the healing properties of specific frequency ratios.

Several features characterize Dīkṣitar's Śruti practice:

1. Extended Gamaka (Oscillation): Dīkṣitar's melodic style features long, slow oscillations around each note — the note is not attacked directly but approached from below or above, touched, sustained with gentle vibrato, and then released. This gamaka technique ensures that the full Śruti range of each note is explored, activating all the microtonal healing properties associated with that note's Śruti region.

2. Kampita (Shake): A specific type of gamaka in which the note oscillates rapidly between two adjacent Śrutis. This kampita creates a shimmer effect — the note seems to glow or vibrate with an inner light. Therapeutically, kampita activates the nervous system at a very subtle level, producing a state of alert relaxation that is ideal for healing.

3. Śruti-Sāhitya Alignment: Dīkṣitar carefully aligns the emotional weight of the Sanskrit syllable with the Śruti weight of the note. Heavy, resonant syllables (those with anusvāra, long vowels, or compound consonants) are placed on notes with strong Śruti presence (Sa, Ma, Pa); light, agile syllables are placed on notes with delicate Śruti presence (Ga, Ni). This alignment creates a phonemic-musical coherence that amplifies the healing effect of both the text and the melody.

Case Study: "Akṣayaliṅga Vibho" (Rāga Śaṅkarābharaṇam, Melakarta 29)

This kṛti, addressed to Śiva in the form of the Akṣayaliṅga at Tiruvārūr, is one of Dīkṣitar's most celebrated compositions. Let us examine its Śruti profile:

Rāga Śaṅkarābharaṇam (Melakarta 29): Sa, R2, G3, M1, Pa, D2, N3

This is the Indian equivalent of the Western major scale — the brightest, most balanced, most universally appealing of all scales. Its Śruti profile is:

444
THE MICROTONAL ANATOMY OF HEALING SOUND

  • Sa (Śrutis 1-4): Full, stable tonic — grounding

  • R2 (Śruti 7, Rati, "pleasure"): Warm, pleasant second — comforting

  • G3 (Śruti 9, Krodhā): In this context, not "angry" but bright and confident — the major third radiating sunlight

  • M1 (Śruti 13, Mārjanī, "purifying"): The pure, natural fourth — cleansing

  • Pa (Śrutis 14-17): Full, stable fifth — harmonizing

  • D2 (Śruti 20, Ramyā, "beautiful"): The warm, beautiful sixth — soothing

  • N3 (Śruti 22, Kṣobhiṇī): The leading tone, creating gentle upward aspiration — elevating

The overall therapeutic profile is one of comprehensive balance — grounding and elevating, comforting and energizing, purifying and beautifying. Śaṅkarābharaṇam is the rāga-equivalent of a broad-spectrum tonic — it addresses the whole person, bringing every aspect of body, mind, and soul into alignment.

The sāhitya "Akṣayaliṅga Vibho" means "O Lord of the Imperishable Liṅga" — identifying Śiva with the eternal, indestructible principle of consciousness. The Sanskrit word "Akṣaya" (imperishable) contains:

  • A (the primordial vowel, activating the throat and chest)

  • Kṣ (the compound consonant, activating the palate and back of the mouth)

  • a (again, open vowel)

  • ya (palatal glide, activating the palate)

This sequence of sounds — open, compound, open, glide — creates a phonemic pattern that opens, contracts, opens, and flows — mirroring the pattern of breathing and the pattern of the heartbeat. The word itself becomes a miniature Prāṇāyāma, a micro-rhythmic exercise that entrains the singer's breath and heartbeat to its pattern.

Combined with the Śruti profile of Śaṅkarābharaṇam, the result is a comprehensive healing experience — the body is tuned by the Śrutis, the breath is entrained by the sāhitya, the mind is focused by the rāga's clarity, and the soul is awakened by the invocation of Śiva.
